Consequently, many users primarily rely on reposts, which are a common lazy way of re-sharing others' tweets with additional comments (Taneva & Dimou, 2010). While reposts can sometimes spread misinformation, they can also spread faster than truthful information (Vosoughi, Roy, & Aral, 2018), which suggests the importance of identifying and organizing important information for users seeking to grasp the development of an event through reposts. In this context, it becomes necessary to study how major information flows can be captured and synthesized within or even across repost trees. A repost tree is a tree structure view of a set of tweets, where the different levels of the tree typically represent how a user's message is forwarded by subsequent users. For instance, in figure 1, the tweets at level 0, also known as level-0 messages, are first-tweet messages by different users (e.g., tweets (a) to (e) in figure 1). response: Social media platforms, such as Twitter, have been recognized for years as a powerful source of data that can help predict social and economic phenomena at the population level (Hung and Goh, 2012; Young and Soroka, 2012; Mitchell et al., 2013; Dodds, 2014; Williams et al., 2020). A variety of studies have used Twitter data to predict outcomes ranging from election results (e.g., Wang et al., 2015), poll results (e.g., Junco et al., 2011), economic indicators (e.g., Malhotra and Stokes, 2013; Voigt et al., 2017), to psychological outcomes such as well-being (Hampton et al., 2013; Mitra and Gilbert, 2014). These predictions can be viewed as "nowcasting" exercises - providing short-term forecasts of certain outcomes, leveraging the temporal and geographical granularity inherent in social media data (Ginsberg et al., 2009). The resulting nowcasts have been shown to predict future outcomes for between 1 to 3 months or even year-over-year trends For instance, a nowcast of Google search trends for flu-like symptoms obtained from location-based Twitter data is significantly associated with CDC reported flu data (Minsker et al., 2020). Despite substantial research and several notable successes, there are limitations and variables at play. One key issue is how language (lexicon) features extracted from tweets relate to population-level outcomes, especially in aggregating millions or billions of user-generated tweets. Most existing approaches consider the "population-level" language features by simply aggregating over all tweets in a given geographic community (e.g., tweets from the entire country, the state, or the county). Such an approach, while simple, could be problematic if one considers the inherent "noise" or diversity of the measured variables - in this case, language usage, which often varies greatly across different individuals within a population. The reliance on population-level aggregation could introduce uninformative or even misleading noise into the language features, which could hinder the predictive power of the nowcasting models. This is especially true if there are subgroups of users within a geographical area that use Twitter for different purposes or exhibit different language preferences. For instance, younger people might tweet more frequently about local events or entertainment, while older populations might use Twitter to discuss policy or community-related issues. This paper proposes a novel approach to building population-level models based on social media text data by aggregating at the user level before summarizing to the population level. However, these annotations can still be noisy and possibly mislabeled. To address this noise, one may use ensemble techniques which can potentially unrealistically inflate the model capacity, therefore increasing overfitting. A more effective approach is to use a smaller yet powerful model on questions labeled by multiple annotators. This approach has shown success in improving and stabilizing the model performance on part-of-speech (POS) tagging and dependency parsing tasks. In this paper, we investigate how to deal with label set variation for question generation task, an emerging task due to its implications in reading comprehension and dialogue systems. We note that, unlike traditional NLP tasks, there is no strict vocabulary or predefined set of labels for questions, despite the existence of ontologies. This allows neural networks to learn directly from available question semantic features instead of relying on hand-crafted or even pre-defined features required by existing approaches. We observe that even though questions annotated under different datasets/standards may share common semantics (such as topics), their form and structure (e.g., grammar, length, vocabulary) can vastly differ. For instance, questions from MRC (Machine Reading Comprehension) data or questions from educational K-12 data can be very different. Our hypothesis is that a well-engineered neural network model can understand the common semantic structures underlying these heterogeneous question sets, while the differences in form can be taken in good part as a kind of "variation". This paper addresses two main challenges. First, we design a neural network model that can effectively use heterogeneous question sets for training, without requiring manually-engineered features or large additional model capacity. We hypothesize that neural networks, with their general representation abilities and ability to automatically extract features from inputs, can adaptively learn from different annotations without getting overwhelmed by variations. Second, we empirically investigate if different neural network architectures and training strategies, e.g. attention mechanisms and multi-task learning, significantly improve performance or generalize better on unseen domains. This is critical as these methods, while popular, are often applied as a "default" without rigorous analysis of their benefits explicitly for heterogeneous annotation scenarios. Third, we report an analysis on the benefits of different training strategies when the data differs across multiple ontologies and labeling styles. In an increasingly online world, multilingual speakers often switch languages within communication chains, and such switches occur not only across paragraphs but even within the same sentence. Most current language identification technology, therefore, faces indispensable challenges. A particular issue is the existence of code-switching – the combination of two or more languages in conversations (Corson, 1993; Myers-Scotton, 2002). In language identification at the level of a sentence or longer, code-switching is mitigated by context that helps keeps the segmentation into language units. However, in mixed language texts where words or word fragments are embedded within a sentence, there is frequently not enough context to identify the language correctly. In this paper, we present our approach to word level language identification in online multilingual communications. Our proposed method benefits from language modeling and contextual information to accurately assign a single language ID to individual words. We build language models using a collection of monolingual texts and dictionaries for each language of interest. These models form the basis of our initial word-level language identification, which can be viewed as a simplification of the problem to a multi-label classification task. However, the problem is not that simple. Human language often presents context-dependence and ambiguity that cannot be fully captured by word-level models alone. Therefore, we recognize the need to incorporate contextual information while maintaining simplicity and scalability. To address this issue, we introduce two new metrics for evaluating the performance of our model. The first metric measures the ability to keep distinct languages separate while the second measures the correct identification of mixed code-switching instances. They are ubiquitous online platforms where users can share their ideas, communicate with each other, and participate in various activities. Consequently, social networks have become a fertile ground for various research areas including organization behavior, social influence, information diffusion, and network security. An underlying assumption in much of this research is that the network structure of the involved social network is accurately and completely known. However, this assumption can often not be met. In recent years, graph alignment has emerged as an important area of research due to its wide applications. It has been applied to areas like network comparison, data integration, and weighted graph matching. The conceptually simplest form of graph alignment is unweighted graph alignment, which involves finding a permutation of the nodes of the second graph such that the two graphs are maximally similar. However, in many practical scenarios, the similarities and differences between graphs are characterized by weights (attachments) on the edges between the nodes. Hence, we are primarily interested in weighted graph alignment, where the goal is to find a permutation of the nodes of the graph B that maximizes the "alignment score" which depends on the assumed metric between the edges of the two graphs. response: Certainly, here is the introduction for the paper on Improved Semantic Parsers for If-Then Statements: Introduction The accelerated development of digital personal assistants (DPA) has brought natural language processing (NLP) to the center stage of tech innovation. For instance, voice-controlled assistants such as Siri, Google Assistant, and Alexa enable users to access information, modify settings, and complete tasks using everyday language. But while speech recognition (translating spoken words into text) has made great strides, a bigger challenge lies in the realm of machine understanding (translating text into a set of machine-executable instructions). In order for a DPA to act on a user's request, it must first be able to 'understand' the request’s meaning. This process is called semantic parsing. Semantic parsing is the task of translating natural language (NL) to a symbolic representation, such as formal logic, weighted finite state transducers, or a programming language. For personal assistants, this often means translating user queries into a certain form of controlled natural language known as Knowledge Bases (KBs) or also known as knowledge graphs. Many user commands to DPAs are in the form of rules or scripts, typically written in the "if-then" format or as conditional statements. For example, "if this event happens, then perform this action." However, these "if-then" statements are often expressed in a form that is ambiguous or context-dependent, making them hard to interpret for machines. For instance, consider the following plausible rule for a DPA: "If it is raining outside, then close the windows." To execute this rule, the device needs to understand exactly what is meant by "it is raining outside" and "close the windows." It must map these natural language expressions to some defined entities (measuring devices, actuators, etc.) that can be controlled or queried. Therefore, understanding how to parse such rules effectively is crucial for enabling DPAs to act upon user commands accurately and efficiently. The task of semantic parsing for "if-then" rules, while having a variety of applications beyond DPAs (including web search, conversational interfaces, and even software verification), presents its own unique challenges. For example, the presence of vague concepts ("raining outside"), implicit assumptions about the system state and available actions, and the need to handle conditionals – where the condition may be complex or unevaluated. Existing semantic parsers often struggle with these challenges. Conventional techniques, such as rule-based systems or dependency parsing, can map simple conditionals fairly straightforwardly, but they are often inadequate for more complex or ambiguous expressions. Neural network models, such as those used in deep parsing or graph-based semantic role labeling, have shown promise but are still limited by the quality of training data, overfitting to particular datasets, or inability to generalize across different forms of "if-then" statements. To this end, this paper explores a series of improvements designed to enhance the effectiveness of semantic parsers specifically for "if-then" statements. Our work builds on both conventional and neural network models, with a particular emphasis on ways to improve structure prediction – the process of inferring the logical, executable structure from an "if-then" rule expressed in natural language. We will cover successful techniques for handling conditionals, including better ways to represent and predict compound or nonliteral conditions. For instance, using rule-based systems, we might introduce more granularity in recognizing "raining outside" as a combination of weather predictions and location-based sensors, rather than a single, abstract condition. Additionally, we will discuss methods for improving generalization and reducing overfitting.

response: Social media platforms, online forums, and web-based discussion spaces have become increasingly popular in recent years as primary sources of information and as platforms for social interaction. While these online spaces offer many benefits, they also pose significant challenges particularly when it comes to content organization and information organization. Asynchronous, multi-threaded, and multi-party conversations, a hallmark of online discussions, compound these organizational challenges. Unlike conversations in face-to-face interactions where gestures and simultaneous speech can make it clear who responds to whom, online text-only conversations often lack clear cues to signal the initiation of a thread and the response to it. The lack of these cues keeps analysts struggling to deconstruct and understand the conversational structure. Initiation-response pairs are a fundamental building block of conversations. By structuring verbal interactions into pairs of initiation and response, analysts can better understand the conversation flow and the interactions between participants. This semantic structure serves as a scaffold for a comprehensive study of the discussed content. As such, automated identification of initiation-response pairs holds great potential for understanding the dynamics and semantic structure of online discussions at scale. However, identifying initiation-response pairs in online text-based discussions is a non-trivial task. Unlike in face-to-face interactions or synchronous online discussions, where timing can help infer initiative and response or even where explicit signaling is possible, asynchronous and multi-party discussions on online platforms present unique challenges. In this paper, we propose to address the challenge of identifying initiation-response pairs in multi-threaded, multi-party online discussions. Specifically, we tackle this problem as a pairwise ranking task, where we are given two dialogue edges and we aim to rank them: (i) the probability that the left edge prompts the right one, and (ii) the probability that the right edge responds to the left one. We first justify the focus on this problem. Understanding initiation-response pairs offers two key benefits: (1) it helps in reorganizing the discussion content for better readability, which can improve content finding and understanding, and (2) it can be used to build higher-level structured summaries that capture the main points, debates, and evolving discussions within the community. We next outline the technical foundations of our proposed approach. The core of our method is based on Latent Semantic Analysis (LSA). LSA is a well-established method used in distributional semantic modeling where words are represented in a high-dimensional vector space where semantically similar words are close to each other. Specifically, we propose a novel variant of LSA that addresses the challenge posed by uncommon words, which are often critical in signaling initiation-response links but are deemphasized in standard LSA models due to their infrequent use. Uncommon words such as "contrary to" or "However" can serve as strong indicators of a responsive or rebuttal type of dialogue. Our enhanced LSA variant is designed to better capture these less common but often semantically crucial words while still leveraging the more frequent words that typify the response or initiation. Our work builds on prior research but addresses specific limitations of existing work. While the use of LSA or other distributional semantic models is common in natural language processing applications, these models primarily deal with content similarity between sentences or documents. One indispensable technique for exploiting monolingual data is back-translation (Snover et al., 2006;Matusov et al., 2009;Maren and Subramanian, 2009), which was originally proposed to improve word alignment (Koehn and Och, 2003). In its most basic form, back-translation consists of first generating a large target language corpus by translating monolingual data using a pre-trained NMT model and then adding this corpus back into the training of the same or a related NMT model. This simple technique has been shown in many language pairs and datasets to result in substantial improvements in translation quality. Despite the success of back-translation, relatively little is known about its underlying mechanisms and when it works best. For example, how large a training set is required? What is the effect of various back-translation methods? How does it interact with other techniques such as data augmentation or domain adaptation? What is the relationship between back-translation and actual bitext training data? Our work is divided into four parts. First, we investigate how effective back-translation is while adding increasing amounts of synthetic data to the training set. We evaluate its effectiveness across eight language pairs with varied sizes of parallel data, and compare it carefully to using genuine (bitext) data. Our results suggest that back-translation can still lead to gains even when in practice the size of synthetic data exceeds that of parallel data. Second, we explore various methods to generate synthetic data for back-translation, including sampling from the candidates provided by the model and the use of noisy beam outputs. We also consider the choice between greedy and beam search based approaches. We find that the choice of method is surprisingly crucial, and methods that involve sampling or noise (which increase the diversity of generated sentences) tend to give better gains than ones based on either greedy or beam search. Third, we analyze the quality of various synthetic data generators and compare it to genuine bitext. response: Training natural language processing (NLP) models reliably on large datasets is inherently challenging due to variability in data quality and distribution. The K-fold cross validation (CV) technique is widely used to estimate model performance by randomization and the resulting estimates of various evaluation measures. However, due to its stochastic nature, the K-fold CV can produce unstable estimates, particularly for NLP questions where the dataset distribution and context can significantly affect performance. This stochasticity can lead to suboptimal model parameter selection and parameter tuning. A useful and yet under-explored alternative to mitigate variability in K-fold CV is J-K-fold cross validation (J-K-fold CV), where J independent K-fold CVs are used to estimate model performance, reducing the variance in estimates. However, the adoption of J-K-fold CV for model selection and tuning in NLP is not as prevalent due to the added computational cost. This work bridges this gap by adapting J-K-fold CV for NLP model parameter tuning and investigating the importance of choosing the correct J and K values. The primary goal of this paper is to show that J-K-fold CV can efficiently reduce variance in evaluations, leading to better model parameter choices that are less sensitive to chance and more generalizable. To achieve this, we conduct experiments on a diverse set of NLP tasks, including sentiment analysis, part-of-speech (POS) tagging, and document classification. The dataset used throughout is the popular IMDB dataset, while the POS task benefits from the Wall Street Journal (WSJ) corpus and several sentiment analysis tasks (including general and specialized sentiment classification) use sentiments annotated by the Stanford Sentiment Treebank (SST). In addition to exploring the effect of varying J and K on performance in these tasks, we investigate the computational trade-offs of using J-K-fold CV versus traditional K-fold and other methods of variance reduction like bootstrapping and stratified sampling. Our approach is structured around the following steps: 1. **Adaptation and extension of J-K-fold CV to parameter tuning**: We adapt the J-K-fold CV technique into a method for parameter tuning in NLP models. Our primary objective here is to base parameter selection not on single K-fold CV estimates, but on the more stable mean and spread across J trials. 2. **Investigating J and K**: We systematically vary the number of folds (K) and the number of J trails to analyze how these affect model performance estimates and parameter selections. By doing this for a variety of NLP tasks, we aim to identify general guidelines for choosing J and K for different types of models and tasks. 3. **Computational and practical considerations**: We explore the computational cost of J-K-fold CV and compare it with other variance reduction techniques. This includes comparing with techniques like bootstrapping and stratified sampling plus evaluating whether these alternatives can match or surpass J-K-fold CV in utility-cost trade-off for NLP applications. 4. **Empirical evaluation on a variety of NLP tasks**: We apply our J-K-fold CV tuning method to a broad set of NLP problems: sentiment analysis (both generic and targeted, e.g., product vs. movie sentiment), part-of-speech tagging, and document classification. The target across these tasks is to verify that J-K-fold CV parameters can be tuned to outperform or at least match the predictive performance of models tuned with less stable methods, while also offering improved generalizability. The central hypothesis we test through these experiments is that by reducing variance, J-K-fold CV can lead to more robust and better generalizing models. These applications range from natural language processing (NLP) such as machine translation, question answering and information retrieval, to computational linguistics, including parsing, semantic analysis and corpus-based linguistics research. Despite the existence of a number of sizeable corpora designed for cross-linguistic comparison (e.g., parallel corpora and comparable corpora), idiomatic and technical terms that may not share structural resemblance with equivalents in the target language are seldom easily identifiable. This issue is especially pronounced for languages that structurally differ extensively from each other, such as English and Chinese. Therefore, training translators and scholars, as well as developing reliable machine translation systems for such language pairs, need automatic alignment of technical terms. We present a method that tackles this issue by combining both string and semantic context similarity for term alignment from comparable corpora. We argue that term translation clues are well-documented to be multifaceted and partly intermingled, so the best approach requires leveraging both sub-lexical (character-level) string similarity, which ensues from the orthographic characteristics of technical terms and their general tendency to be multi-component and modular, as well as contextual or semantic similarity, which is often a key determinant of term meaning. String similarity, when decomposed into n-gram character compositionality, allows capturing the sequential structure of terms, while the context similarity benefits from existing distributional learning-based techniques that estimate term embeddings or representations, based on the surrounding words or phrases. Our key innovation is to formalize the combination of these two translation clues into a unified, learned model. In this task, summarizers are often trained using sequence-to-sequence models (Seq2Seq), where a decoder constructs a summary phrase by phrase based on the training data. Despite its success, this approach exhibits a number of limitations. First, some summaries may tend to introduce new and often redundant information while failing to retain important words or relations from the original text that may critically contribute to the meaning of the content. Second, there are cases where the structure and meaning of the source sentences are not properly preserved in the summary, leading to a loss of significance or unintended meaning distortion, especially in cases where complex structures or key relationships are intertwined with verbal content. These issues are more pronounced when the summaries are too concise, or when the source is rich in structural semantic features beyond simple word tokens. Structurally rich language involves dependency or constituent structures that are well-documented to be crucial in conveying meaning and understanding of human language. The language of complex documents (such as academic papers, creative writing, etc.) often relies on these structures to build meaning, convey relationships between ideas, or to perform various discourse functions such as referential linking or contrast or even inferential reasoning. They allow for modeling the structure of a language, assigning probabilities to grammar rules, thus capturing uncertainty in language generation. These features make PCFGs particularly useful for applications that involve probabilistic prediction in language, such as speech recognition, machine translation, and language modeling. In some of these applications, certain information about the portion of a language being processed is important, for instance, the probability of a specific substring (or "infix") appearing at a particular point in a sentence or utterance. Past research has addressed the problem of infix probability computation, but has often made simplifying assumptions that limit the generality of the solution. response: Language models are fundamental components of many natural language processing (NLP) tasks (Bengio et al., 2003;Jurafsky and Martin, 2009). They estimate the probabilities of token sequences in a given text corpus, therefore providing a indispensable training signal for other NLP models. Current state-of-the-art language models, such as recurrent neural networks (RNN) (Mikolov et al., 2010) and Transformer (Vaswani et al., 2017), learn the structure and probabilistic patterns from a given corpus without explicit knowledge of named entities (NE) within the text. However, most real-world texts, especially in domains such as news articles, research papers, and programming code, include significant amounts of NEs - such as people’s names, locations, organizations, and programming entities. These NE names can be highly specific, and thus appear infrequently in a training corpus, making it difficult for purely character-level or word-level language models to learn the patterns and distributions of these NE names. Furthermore, NE names often carry syntactic and semantic relationships with the surrounding words, which traditional language models may not capture effectively. For instance, in English, "apple" or "apple inc" are both valid words, but contextually, they have different meanings and relationships with surrounding words. Therefore, to create a robust text generation model, predicting entity names while maintaining semantic coherence with surrounding text is essential. Despite the importance of NEs in text, most current training datasets do not explicitly tag or distinguish entity names for training language models, or tag them as 'out-of-vocabulary' (OOV) tokens. As a result, current language models often underperform when dealing with NE-rich texts or achieve only incremental improvements by using simple strategies such as adding infrequent words to the vocabulary. response: Analyzing language in context has gained much attention both in theoretical linguistics and in computational linguistic applications. To analyze context today, nearly every system or algorithm relies to some extent on the assumption that language can be understood at least partially if not entirely on the basis of its internal properties, including its syntactic structure or the meaning of the words, phrases, clauses, or sentences that are part of it. In contrast to these internal properties, context and discourse, broadly defined, are the properties that relate a piece of language to the language right before or after it, or independent of its internal structure and meaning. The study of discourse has a long history in linguistics. It is well known from knowledge source theory (Kehler, 2002) that many properties of discourse structure, such as presupposition or focus assignment, are underdetermined by just the internal properties of sentences. This means that beyond understanding the precise meaning of each sentence in a piece of language we need additional context to understand what the speaker actually meant when they produced this exact sequence of linguistic elements. This underdetermined nature makes discourse handling particularly difficult for computational approaches. In the past, computational approaches have been primarily focused on handling well-structured data. As for achieving the goal of automatic discourse processing or information structure processing, there have been numerous attempts to develop automated discourse and information structure tagging or discourse role labeling (e.g., the DISCORTE project (Hardt 1999; Hardt and Scott in press; Hardt and Traum 2005; Traum and Ng 2008; Strube 2004), studies focusing on specific phenomena such as focus structure, discourse structure, anaphora resolution in discourse, as well as more general discourse processing tasks such as discourse role labeling or discourse segmentation. However, progress in these efforts has been somewhat slow and many of the annotated datasets that have been used for developing models for different aspects of discourse and information structure, e.g. the Wikipedia-based or CNN datasets (e.g. Strube and Hahn 2016) are relatively small in size. This lack of progress for certain discourse and information structure phenomena is mainly due to the fact that traditional discourse and information structure phenomena are less well-defined in terms of formalistic features than concepts such as parts of speech, dependency structure, argument structure, or sense of a word. This does not mean that some formal features or evidence do not exist or cannot be used in automatic discourse and structure analyses. As we will later discuss, indeed various information structural phenomena are potentially informative for an automatic focus parser. Formal theoretical approaches to the study of information structure exist almost as long as the study of information structure itself. Their method, based on the Ising spin model [1], makes use of the features of connectedness of words in a matrix and the derived ising-like model for the positivity/negativity of a word following a particular co-occurrence pattern. [1] They discovered a temperature-like parameter and reported a phase transition when this parameter was optimized. It has since been confirmed and improved by many others, including Okanohara and Kajikawa (2006), Malpass and Croft (2006), He and Croft (2010) For a survey of this line of work and its relevance to semantic orientation extraction, see He and Croft (2010). The authors assumed that the model may eventually reach a stable point in the phase transition at the optimal temperature, which led to plausible performance on a variety of polarity estimation tasks (e.g., for determining semantic orientation, or for distinguishing positive vs. negative texts). This idea has proven to be a very fruitful and elegant way of learning sentiment based on word co-occurrence, and a plethora of improvements and extensions over the past decade have built upon this foundation. For a long time, research on textual entailment has been dominated by shallow features such as lexical matching, conjunctions, and basic anaphora resolution, while the deeper structures and aspects of discourse are often inadequately represented or entirely neglected within these approaches. However, the importance of incorporating richer discourse features has been gaining traction over recent years (e.g., Bifone et al., 2011; Maleki et al., 2015). Among these, the machine learning methods have been widely used in the past decade and shown better summarization quality as they are capable of learning from observed data and adapting to new tasks without human effort. Learning-based approach typically rely on feature engineering and optimization techniques to select salient sentences, and then to predict summary structures based on these selected sentences. These methods need to learn from a very large corpus in order to tune their parameters to achieve good performance. However, among the features that current methods used, very little study has been done on "coherence" of the summary. response: Named Entity Recognition (NER) involves detecting and classifying named entities mentioned in unstructured text into predefined categories. Traditionally, the task of NER is based on machine learning algorithms such as Support Vector Machines (SVMs), Conditional Random Fields (CRFs) or deep learning approaches like Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) and Recurrent Neural Networks (RNNs) coupled with Long Short-Term Memory (LSTMs). However, the performance of these algorithms often significantly depends on the availability of large amounts of labeled training data that is domain-specific. The domain (or class set) for which data is available keeps changing as new domains emerge or existing ones evolve. Therefore, training an NER system on one domain and applying it on another without adaptation can lead to decreased performance due to significant differences in features such as word usage, punctuation, and named entities between domains. This is the domain adaptation problem in the context of NER. The domain adaptation problem can be particularly challenging in scenarios where the target domain is expected to contain named entity categories that are absent or rare in the source domain. For instance, applying a NER system trained on a general domain such as news articles on another domain like medical text may not perform well since the latter might have specific medical or biological entities that are absent in general domains. One effective way to deal with this challenge is to use bootstrapping, a semi-supervised learning technique that leverages assumed unlabeled data to boost the classification performance of the learning model. However, typical bootstrapping approaches, also known as self-training, can have difficulty adapting to new domains because they equate features for which the model is confident as informative, without considering whether those features are relevant in the target domain. Assuming that both labeled (source) and unlabeled (target) data are available, and the goal is to improve the performance of NER in the target domain, domain adaptive bootstrapping seeks to address this issue. The idea is to intelligently select which instances from the unlabeled target data to label (or bootstrap from) in such a way that they serve as bridges between the source and target domains. One key concern is the extent to which various composition models can capture meaning at the level of sentences. A particular challenge comes from the need to assess whether – and how questions such as "What is the meaning of a sentence if the meaning of its parts are already known"? can be addressed with a given vector representation. response: Automatic discourse analysis is a crucial task in natural language processing (NLP) that can have significant effects on several downstream applications. For instance, it can improve the quality of summarization (Way, 2004), question answering (Potts et al., 2003), or other applications that rely on understanding the content of text at the discourse level. One of the most established frameworks for discourse analysis is Rhetorical Structure Theory (RST) (Mann and Thompson, 1988), where the primary goal is to represent the structure and meaning of a text as a labeled, hierarchical tree called a Discourse Tree (DT) (Figure 1). The leaves of a DT correspond to Elementary Discourse Units (EDUs), which are contiguous and independently meaningful text spans. EDUs are connected by a rhetorical relation, derived directly from relationships among semantic entities in the text. The sample tree in Figure 1 shows four EDUs linked by two relations: Hence and Antithesis. The exploration of such semantic relationships among language components at the discourse level is appealing because it can unveil the underlying intent of the text. Previous work on automatic discourse analysis has mainly focused on two tasks: discourse segmentation and discourse parsing. Discourse segmentation or EDU boundary detection is the task of identifying the boundaries of EDUs in a given text. Discourse parsing seeks to link these EDUs into a DT by identifying appropriate rhetorical relations while deciding whether an EDU is a NUCLEUS (central to the author's intended meaning) or a SATELLITE (secondary or supporting). One of the limitations of current approaches is that they treat the tasks of discourse segmentation and discourse parsing separately. For example, the widely adopted approach based on sequential Markov models (SM) (Soricut and Marcu, 2003) doesn't learn the disambiguation of EDUs and how they should be connected until after the segmentation step has occurred. Furthermore, these approaches make strong independence assumptions between the different characteristics of the DT constituents, and they do not guarantee a globally optimal solution. Work has been primarily centered on adapting two key models: the translation model (TM) and the language model (LM). However, a third, equally crucial component of the SMT system that has received relatively little attention in the adaptation literature is the reordering model (RM), which guides how phrases are ordered during translation. Phrase-based SMT systems rely on the RM to reorder word order during translation. Typically, the RM is trained using a small amount of in-domain data, with very little focus on adaptation. We concentrate on abstractive approaches which can generate summaries that do not necessarily appear in the original documents being summarized. Opinions expressed through natural language are variously called 'responses', 'feedback' or 'reviews'. People have opinions about, e.g., restaurants, movies, hotels, products, and so on. The abundance of such opinions and reviews offers companies valuable access into public sentiments and preferences that they can then use to make better informed business decisions. To aggregate such opinions, though, and gain insight from them, extracted summaries of these opinions can be particularly useful. However, opinion summaries are often redundant, wordy, and contain a great deal of superfluous information. These problems need to be addressed to have any chance at conducting meaningful Sentiment Analysis (SA), to accurately understand opinion polarity. This paper presents a novel graph-based approach (Opinosis) for abstractive summarization that specifically targets highly redundant text. Our approach is motivated by observations of the nature of opinions and reviews expressed via natural language. Typically, opinions and user reviews are long, verbose, and often similar resulting in a lot of redundancy. As such, Opinosis can be interpreted as a way or a framework to intuitively generate a reduced form of the original text while preserving as much information as possible. Our graph-based framework is highly efficient and has been specifically designed to handle multi-document summaries where the individual documents themselves are sets of opinions. We show that our approach to opinion summarization can effectively handle the problem of redundancy and generates relatively short summaries (average of 8-10 sentences) that are significantly more readable than baseline methods. The quality and usefulness of the generated summaries are validated by means of human evaluations, and a set of computational baselines. The remainder of this paper is organized as follows: in Section II, we describe related work; in Section III, we introduce the Graph-Based framework Opinosis and discuss the design rationale; in Section IV, we discuss the experimental setup and measured evaluation results together with human judgment; in Section V, we outline applications of the proposed summarization approach; in Section VI, we present some conclusions and possible avenues for future work. Many of today's opinion extraction techniques are often based on the assumption that individual documents are long and diverse. However, user reviews of products or services – on aggregators such as Amazon or in online forums – are often highly redundant in nature. This work takes a principled and feature-rich approach to identify cognate sets across related languages that may potentially share a common language of origin or protoword. However, due to the vast quantity and complexity of texts, such annotation processes are typically time-consuming and expensive. This is particularly evident in the domain of sentence semantic equivalence identification (SSEI) and question answering systems, where a manual annotation of paraphrased sentences or questions and answers could be prohibitively expensive. This paper aims to tackle part of the annotation challenge by presenting the Bank Question (BQ) corpus — a large-scale, manually-annotated Chinese corpus for sentence semantic equivalence identification (SSEI). The BQ corpus contains 120,000 question pairs from a 1-year online bank custom service logs. These verbal interactions often result in a very similar set of semantic interpretations, despite the differing linguistic expressions used by both customers and bank customer service representatives. As such, our corpus provides a valuable resource for identifying sentence semantic equivalence that is closely aligned with customer service communication. To ensure a high-quality and efficient annotation process, we proposed and implemented a creative yet systematic approach. First, we used Word Mover's Distance (WMD) based Affinity Propagation (AP) clustering algorithm to group questions or questions and answers that are highly correlated in meaning. WMD is a similarity measure between two documents that is based on their word vectors in a shallow neural network embedding space . However, the AP clustering algorithm can label the data points with the most representative point as a cluster center, which we can consider as the ‘questions with the same intent’. By applying WMD to the questions (or answers), we significantly reduce the manual labeling workload as the annotators only need to check if each cluster is indeed of the same intent and if there are questions that belong to that same intent category but are likely to be mislabeled. To further optimize the manual annotation process, we employed two rounds of clustering and labeling to identify potential intent clusters and eliminate or merge irrelevant ones. The first round clustering helped to identify potential intent clusters together with questions that did not belong to any matched answer. For the second round, we applied cluster refinement to merge or split clusters based on manual evaluation. Following the clustering-based and semi-automated approach, a team of 5 trained annotators were then asked to assign each cluster into one of 10 pre-defined semantic categories. Hence, deep learning models that can make better use of various forms of unannotated (or partially annotated) data have become increasingly important (Hermann and Blunsom, 2014; Shen et al., 2018). Pre-training of distributed word representations (Mikolov et al., 2013) and language models (Peters et al., 2018) on unlabeled data can improve performance. However, task-specific architectures and training data are usually still required. This is especially true for sequence-dependent tasks such as dependency parsing, where the ability to capture word connections is crucial. Sentences are not like isolated word sequences; relationships among semantic entities (i.e., words) can convey a lot of the information required to understand the structure. Dependency parsing is traditionally seen as a syntactic task, which means the objective is to generate a dependency parse tree that correctly captures the syntactic structure of a sentence. But the task often involves similar components as semantic role labeling (SRL) or semantic parsing, in that the next word in the derivation is influenced not only by the current word but also by the relationship between symbols. Recent work suggests SRL can benefit from multitask learning with contextualized word representations (Durrett and Klein, 2014). Stages at which the model has yet to make predictions are called decision variables. Issues can arise if the model is over-eager in assigning features to decision variables, leading to sparsity, especially if word embeddings do not capture inherent word connections. Implicit word connections (IWC) are the hypothetical contexts that help to predict "which word depends on which other word" implicitly from unlabeled data. If the model is inconsistent in assigning IWC to contextual dependencies, this can result in degraded performance, as dependency parsers are sensitive to the order and relations among words in the sentence. Our goal is to explicitly learn IWC from unlabeled data. The learning of IWC is implicit in the sense that we do not require task-specific supervision or gold-standard dependency labels. Instead, we aim to capture IWC by changing the architecture to induce more meaningful interaction between words. A common advanced dependency parser uses a transition-based approach with arc-standard (or arc-hiearchical) features, but these models do not naturally capture sequential relationships among words over zero-order or higher-order dependencies except through feature engineering designed to codify the theoretical intuition about the possible dependencies. We propose an alternative based on a single attention-based layer. We use a self-attention mechanism (Vaswani et al. (2017)) to predict fine-grained connections. Each word is attended to by every word in the sentence to form a temporal relationship that can capture word connections. Depending on how they are defined, MWEs can include phrasal verbs, collocations, idioms, and fixed phrases of various types. A particular and challenging subclass of MWEs is the Contiguous Multiword Expressions (CMEs), which are MWEs where the components are contiguous in the surface word sequence (Striegnitz and Spann, 2008). Due to their high frequency and importance in languages (e.g. Stajner, 2007), handling CMEs correctly has become an essential part of any practical NLP application. These links can be of various types, such as subject, object, or modifier. Dependency parsing can provide detailed information about the syntactic structure which is useful for language understanding and applications such as information extraction, question answering, and machine translation. Recent advances have introduced many effective dependency parsing approaches (Clark and Manning, 2003), with their own strengths and weaknesses, especially in handling CMEs. One common limitation is that many systems treat MWEs as "black boxes," assigning the expected shallow structures to them without capturing their internal syntactic structure. This can lead to inaccuracies and awkward syntactic analyses. response: Training neural networks with large knowledge bases poses two major challenges: (1) efficient neural embedding of knowledge bases, (2) sufficient training samples for statistical estimation of encoder and decoder models. We propose Conditional Focused (CFO) neural networks that address both of these challenges. CFO first uses focus prediction and neural question rewriting to identify relevant knowledge in the questions. Then it uses cross-modal (question and knowledge) information to learn an effective neural question representation, while using a sequence-to-sequence (seq2seq) framework to generate answers. In Table 1, we compare our approach with existing methods that use neural networks for answering factoid questions with knowledge bases. We also provide an analysis of the difficulty of different types of question in Table 2. Experiments show that our proposed CFO model achieves 75.7% accuracy, significantly outperforming existing methods (Plus, semantic parsing, attention-based weighted scoring). Our proposed CFO model consists of an encoder that reads the question and focuses on a subset of information, and a decoder that generates an answer. Encoder: Our encoder first reads the user question, then predicts whether it should focus on a specific sentence in the knowledge base. Figure 2 illustrates the sequential structure of the encoder and the flow of information. The focus prediction is a binary classification problem on the identified symbols. We use a deep recurrent neural network (LSTM with 128 units), assumed to learn the distributed representation of the question so far and make the decision. Decoder: The decoder reads the knowledge base and the predicted focus (if any), using a seq2seq model to generate answers (see Figure 3). This allows it to model the different representations in knowledge base as well as the question structure when generating the answer, and avoids the need for large amounts of training data. Training: The training uses candidates provided in the knowledge base for each question. For questions without such information, we use cross-entropy loss to predict answer spans in the knowledge base. The CFO model was trained together with both a focus prediction model and a question answering decoder. The learning objective is a combination of cross-entropy for focus prediction and cross-entropy plus regularization for decoder. Evaluation: We use a collection of 108,000 manually reviewed questions answered by humans. To handle more complex questions, we also present in Section 4 several proposed modifications to the CFO model, including allowing the decoder to use attention on the focus information or integrating additional semantic information such as dependency graphs. Conclusion: This work proposes the Conditional Focused (CFO) neural networks framework to leverage large-scale knowledge bases for question answering. Our experiments and results demonstrate that focusing inherently increases the efficiency of retrieving knowledge from large-scale knowledge bases and improves performance. However, the work also leaves several questions open: • Can we integrate typological or semantic information from the knowledge base into CFO? • How does the performance of CFO model change if we use unsupervised or weakly supervised training data? • How can the results of question answering with knowledge bases from different domains be combined efficiently? response: Discriminative Reranking of Discourse Parses Using Tree Kernels Introduction Discourse structure represents the relationships and dependencies among propositions within a text and is crucial for natural language understanding tasks such as information extraction, question answering, summarization and discourse parsing. Discourse parsing can be viewed as the problem of constructing a discourse tree (a directed acyclic graph) that represents hierarchical and relational structures between texts. Besides improving narrative coherence, this permits access to deeper understanding and links sentences to higher-level structural elements, thus enriching text representation and facilitating downstream tasks. However, while probabilistic parsers can create relatively accurate discourse trees given a set of input sentences, the search space remains large and the likelihood estimates, which are optimization objectives for such parsers, can be unreliable due to the complexity of the problem. This is especially true when dealing with real-world datasets derived from news or web text, which tend to be longer, more varied in structure, and contain noise. To this end, reranking has emerged as a practical technique for improving the accuracy of discourse parsing systems (Johns and Resnick,2007;Smith et al., 2009;Clark et al., 2013), traditionally at the level of or above sentences. Reranking re-evaluates the original decision and selects from the top candidates using features not available or less refined in the initial probabilistic models. The features assumed in the reranking system should capture syntactic, semantic, and higher-level discourse features that help distinguish between the plausible trees derived from the initial parser. However, using distinct features for reranking can lead to less focused models that fail to generalize across datasets or languages. response: Multi-label classification, which allows each sample to be assigned to multiple categories, has been an area of research for several decades. Its accelerated development was fostered by the rapidly increasing use of high-dimensional data, e.g., the number of tags on web-pages (e.g., video labels), words in a document, and micro-blog content (e.g., questions or status updates). In traditional multi-label classification (MLC), a model is trained over a "gold" set containing a large number of samples (e.g., web-pages with thousands of word-embeddings and set labels) and is then evaluated on a "testing" set. However, in many real-world applications, we are interested in predicting labels which are not contained in the training set at all; these are called zero-shot labels. Even if a model was trained over a very large "gold" set, there may be labels that never appear but can still be predicted through the "structure" of the label space. Hence, we have three types of labels in such a problem setting: 1. Frequent labels: labels which appear very frequently in the training set (could be thousands or tens of thousands of samples). 2. Few-shot labels: labels which appear at least once, but not very frequently in the training set. 3. Zero-shot labels: labels which never appear in the training set but are part of the label space (i.e., the set of all possible label assignments in the problem). Multi-label few-and zero-shot label prediction can serve many practical applications. For instance, analyzing patient's electronic health records (EHRs), where patient's ailments, treatments, symptoms, and lab results could all be represented as labels. One could develop a general model that captures all existing clinically confirmed diseases and symptoms but can also predict diseases that have never been diagnosed in that hospital (zero-shot) and the treatment that was prescribed to a patient based on a single previous instance (few-shot). response: Word Sense Disambiguation (WSD) is one of the key challenges in natural language processing. Given that a single word can have multiple senses, determining the intended sense of a word is crucial for many applications, particularly natural language understanding. WSD can be performed at the level of individual words or phrases and can be further classified as a kind of instance-of questions or as semantic role labeling. This work is confined to the former and the all-words version, where the task is to disambiguate every occurrence of a target word without regard to sentence context. The All-Words WSD task is even more challenging due to the fact that the context is not taken into account and most frequent word senses, which are typically easy to model, are not necessarily frequent in the corpus. As such, this task requires a system to model low-frequency senses and often to decide between multiple senses for the same word sense in the sample of data. Traditional WSD approaches, however, often perform poorly on low-frequency senses. This poor performance is linked to the size and content of the training data sets, known as the Distributional Hypothesis (Heylighen, 2003). As proposed by Kaplan & Firth (1957), words that cluster together in the same context are expected to share meaning and sense. When a word sense is rare in the training data, the shallow statistical models that form the backbone of the majority of WSD systems cannot effectively identify good features for that sense. This is evident in the fact that the accuracy on the SemEval 2013 ALL-WORDS WSD task for most systems drops off sharply as one looks at less frequent senses (Saparov, 2013). A key question we pose in this work is: "Could the "balance" of the data set - how well real-world uses of a word reflect the "population" that we might encounter on test data - affect the performance of a WSD system?" In effect, we are asking whether less frequent senses could be more effectively modeled by adjusting a system's training data set to be more representative of the world in which it will operate. Current WSD approaches have largely ignored this potential for adjustment. Instead, the focus has been on collecting a very large amount of data in the hope that eventually all senses will be well-represented. Other efforts aim to find some reasonable subset of words whose senses are well-modeled across the board. However, these approaches typically do not perform better on all senses, focusing instead on improving averages across senses or improving the leading sense, and still often struggle with the tail of the data distribution. This paper presents evidence to the contrary. We argue that more data is not necessarily better, and that the "balancing" of sense distributions in the training data can be as important as, if not more important than, the sheer volume of data. Balance here is understood as how well the observed sense frequencies in a corpus reflect any known or likely distribution that the model will encounter in unseen data. While many researchers have acknowledged that sense distributions matter and may manually customize their corpus based on its properties, these are typically small-scale adjustments. What we propose here is a systematic and principled approach to balancing word senses at the training stage, with the aim of successful generalization across less frequent senses as well. The strategy we employ can be summarized thusly: 1. We define balancing as a model derived from real-world data (such as the distribution of senses within a large corpus) that may not reflect a particular corpus being used for training but represents a "target" distribution, capturing the essential properties of word sense usage

In the accelerated pace of global communication and cultural exchange, languages are being replaced by larger, global languages. This is leading various organizations, including UNESCO, to develop initiatives to preserve languages around the world, through documentation, research, and promotion of endangered languages (Brenzinger and Elsik 2003). Language documentation, the collection and preservation of a language's phonetics, grammar, lexicon, and culture associated with it, involves a significant amount of manual work. The work includes data collection, annotation, and analysis, which are time-consuming and require knowledge and familiarity with linguistic techniques, making the task challenging for non-experts. Field linguists, often with little to no training in computational linguistics, face the additional challenge of working with limited digital infrastructure. This paper presents our work in incrementally learning a dependency parser - a fundamental tool in many NLP systems - with the hope of supporting certain tasks in language documentation, such as syntactic annotation. Dependency Parsing Dependency parsing converts sentences into a graph-structured representation where the grammatical dependencies are depicted as directed edges (attachments) between nodes (words), traditionally interpreted as finite verbs or dependents. Dependency parsing is widely used in NLP applications such as machine translation, information retrieval, and text summarization (Nivre 2016). Modelling dependencies rather than constituent structures benefits these applications as it tends to be more computationally efficient and closer to human comprehension (Oepen et al. 2002). One of the basic tasks in language documentation is annotating texts with syntactic structure. This is akin to dependency-based annotation, as dependency grammars typically represent key grammatical relationships without necessarily capturing all structural complexities (Jackendoff 1997). However, manual annotation of dependency structures is time-consuming and is the bottleneck that limits how much documentation can be achieved, especially in fieldwork, where time and resources are limited. As proposed by (Gillick et al. 2007), Coreference resolution could benefit from a more robust exploration of entity relationships, beyond language models based on standard corpus statistics. One such form of knowledge is discourse-based indicators of coreference, such as antecedent distribution and potential antecedent ranking proposed by (Schwartz 1977) or more recent works on using Forced Alignment and Viterbi on NLP symbols provided by (Yuan et al. 2020). Following this line of thought, the proposed system benefits from incorporating discourse-based signals more explicitly at the mention pair level. Our algorithm builds upon the concept that the most informative relations between entity mentions can guide us towards better coreference decisions without relying on labeled examples or generating complex learned models. Introduction: In natural language processing, identifying polarity of a sentiment word is challenging, especially when the sentiment word collocates with different targets that can influence its polarity. For instance, the word "long" could either refer to "long battery life" (positive) or "long startup time" (negative). The task of determining the correct polarity of such collocations is known as collocation polarity disambiguation. The mainstream approach in collocation polarity disambiguation often relies on the context in which the collocation appears. For example, an algorithm might carefully analyze the surrounding text to decide if "long" is qualifying "battery life" in a positive light or "startup time" in a negative one based on the grammatical structure, words and phrases adjacent to the collocation, and the overall discourse analysis. However, such methods are restricted by the contextual information available and the limitations of human language to contextualize polarity unambiguously. Furthermore, if one aims to utilize labeled datasets for training such methods, the availability of such data is often a bottleneck. The crowd-sourcing of polarity for specific collocations is a time-consuming and expensive process, especially when trying to cover a wide range of collocations across various domains. Thus, an approach that leverages available online resources to generate pseudo contexts could potentially alleviate these limitations. Our Contribution This paper addresses the challenge of collocation polarity disambiguation by proposing an unsupervised framework that leverages web-based pseudo contexts. The central idea is to expand the limited contextual information around collocations by extracting relevant text snippets from the web. These pseudo contexts are hypothetical but based on common patterns in the usage of words. The framework uses these expanded contexts to better disambiguate the polarity of collocations without requiring additional labeled training data or expert annotations. The framework consists of three key components: 1. **Web-based Pseudo Context Collection**: We use web scrapping techniques to collect a corpus of text snippets that include the target word or similar words in collocations with various polarity words. These are pseudo contexts in the sense they are not direct contexts of the collocation instance in question but represent potential usage scenarios that can influence the polarity interpretation. 2. **Polarity Embedding Learning**: From the collected pseudo contexts, we train polarity embeddings for words, including both polarity words and target words. These embeddings capture how a word is associated with different polarities, thereby enabling a representation of the potential polarity of a word in various collocations. 3. **Collocation Polarity Disambiguation**: Using the learned polarity embeddings, the framework predicts the polarity of a candidate collocation.

response: Combining Supervised and Unsupervised Ensembles for Knowledge Base Population Building and updating knowledge bases (KBs) is a fundamental task in Knowledge Representation and Natural Language Processing (NLP). One comprehensive example of such bases is Freebase, which contains extensive facts about entities and relationships. A particular and challenging problem in this domain is Knowledge Base Population (KBP), which aims to automatically populate the KB with new statements and facts. A recent focused workshop at ACL (2015) centred around this problem of KBP, which involves two noteworthy tasks: (1) Cold Start Slot Filling (CSSF), and (2) Tri-lingual Entity Discovery and Linking (TEDL). The CSSF task is to automatically fill-out missing attribute-value pairs in entities identified in previously unseen documents from a new domain. In contrast, the TEDL task aims to jointly discover new entities in multiple languages from big collections of documents, and map each of these new entities to a set of existing entities in a background KB which shares the same language as each discovered entity. These tasks are challenging because of several reasons. First, it often involves entities or entity types that have not been previously encountered. As such, these entities might not have any or very few occurrences in any existing KB. We refer to such entities and entity types as 'cold start' entities. These entities pose a challenge because the traditional machine learning approach of using explicit 'features' based on large scale learning on existing data becomes less effective as there is little or no data available. Second, these tasks often involve analyzing very large amounts of text, which current computational systems might struggle to process in reasonable time. Finally, entities and text in different languages pose an additional challenge in cross-lingual applications, and all contexts must be considered and transferred over through a model. One effective approach to tackle these challenges is to use ensemble methods. These methods combine predictions from several individual models and often provide better performance than any one single model or 'member'. However, different ensembles have different strengths and weaknesses, and together they can capture a variety of information useful to a given task. On one side, supervised ensemble methods leverage explicit training data and integrate by taking averages or majority voting of the member outputs and often offer systematic learning from discriminative features. This is particularly useful if large amounts of labeled examples exist for the task. On the other hand, unsupervised ensemble methods do not rely on explicit labels but usually exploit inherent patterns in the data. Unsupervised ensembles can be used if data is plentiful and no labels are available, or if labels are expensive to obtain. Unsupervised methods often work by grouping related examples together and use these groups to improve model accuracy and stability. In the case of KBP, unsupervised methods can be used for identifying new entities or relations based on statistical properties or co-occurrences in text. In this paper, we propose an innovative approach that combines both supervised and unsupervised ensembles to perform KBP tasks. The literature in the ensemble methods field usually focuses on a single type of ensemble, and rarely explore combinations across supervised, unsupervised, and other categories. response: Training natural language parsers to recover unbounded dependencies is seen as an inherently challenging task, due to their rarity in typical datasets. As a result, most parsers and evaluation protocols do not fully address this problem. In this paper, we address this shortfall by first introducing a new corpus for parsing unbounded dependencies, featuring grammatical constructions from seven categories – which are questions, coordination, relative clauses, modal auxiliaries, phrasal verbs, and two types of appositives (restrictive and non-restrictive). This corpus, called the Unbounded Dependency Recovery (UDR) Corpus, contains approximately 700 sentences, alongside a set of over 1,500 manually annotated unbounded dependency triples. The sentences have been assembled to ensure a diverse representation of the various constructions that can elicit unbounded dependencies. The UDR Corpus is then used to systematically probe the current state-of-the-art of parsing technology by evaluating the performance of a selection of off-the-shelf parsers. Our evaluation employs a strict notion of accuracy – i.e., a dependency is counted as correctly recovered if and only if all three of its components (governor, dependent, and type) are correctly identified. Our results indicate that, across the seven constructions or grammatical categories, the average accuracy for the evaluated parsers is on the range from 25% up to 59%, significantly lower than most reported Parseval scores assumed under the standard POS and dependency parsing tasks. These findings call attention to substantial gaps in several state-of-the-art parsers' performance at recovering unbounded dependencies, suggesting that current benchmark datasets and evaluation methods underestimate the complexity of the parsing problem, especially for retrieval-heavy applications. A more detailed analysis on one of the top-scoring parsers reveals that while it is competent at handling simple cases of unbounded dependencies, it tends to falter where the dependency boundaries are inconsistent across sentences, which appears to be influenced by the excessive usage of global features and assumptions about sentence structure inherent in the parser design. This side of the evaluation unveils that resolving unbounded dependencies, especially of the non-local type, requires a fundamentally different approach to dependency parsing. The implication of these findings touches on the broader evaluation of parsing and NLP tools. While Parseval scores are a convenient and conventional metric, our results suggest they do not capture the full range of a parser’s capabilities. Consequently, relying predominantly on these for system evaluation may unfairly promote over-reliance on structured training data, which tends to overlook the performance on real-world phenomena such as unbounded dependencies. While statistical methods have been well-established for NLP tasks, their performance can be affected adversely by drastically different linguistic structures and usage habits found in non-native corpora. A typical solution to this challenge is constructing or acquiring annotated corpora entirely from learner writings (e.g., Cantoni and Roy, 1999;Johnson, 2000;Guca and Moray, 2011;Chen and Ng, 2013;Nakatani et al., 2017). However, these resources are typically limited in size, and their coverage of features and language varieties is not broad enough to reflect the variability of non-native learner writing. The task of language modeling and error detection can be viewed as a classification problem. A traditional language model provides probability scores over certain language units such as word sequences, which can be used directly as features in a classifier. Error-specific classifiers, on the other hand, are trained specifically for various error types (e.g., article, preposition, verb tense, etc.) or even on error instances in the context of a given context. One problem with this approach, however, is that classifiers trained on native data often fail to identify foreign learner-specific errors, while error-specific classifiers trained on learner data might be overly specialized and overfit to that data, leading to poor generalizability. response: Language models are fundamental components of many natural language processing (NLP) applications, such as speech recognition, machine translation, and text analysis. These models estimate the probability of a sequence of words, and they are commonly represented using n-grams. N-gram models, however, can grow proportionally to the size of the training corpus, leading to size and performance questions when working with large corpuses (Corsaro et al., 2019). The prohibitive size of these models makes their use resource-intensive, especially when querying the model or when porting it to hardware setups with limited resources like mobile devices (Chen and Goodman, 1996; Mikolov et al., 2010). A common approach to address the size problem involves compressing or pruning the n-gram models (Chen and Goodman, 1999; Wang et al., 2018). Pruning methods aim to eliminate less probable n-grams from the model, while compressing methods seek to represent the model more compactly with minimal loss in performance. However, while both methods can lead to smaller models, they can also increase the query time (the time it takes to compute the probability of a given sequence within the model) because the compact representations often require additional processing overhead. To address these issues, Riordan and Altman (1998) introduced a data structure known as the Double-Array. The Double-Array is a data structure that uses two arrays (or parallel arrays) to represent a suffix tree. This structure is particularly useful for n-gram language models because it can represent the tree in significantly less space than traditional methods while maintaining constant time complexity for queries such as substrings and longest common prefix (LCP) calculation. In this paper, we propose an approach to implementing efficiently large-scale language models using the Double-Array data structure. For an n-gram model, this structure allows for fast computation of probabilities for a given n-gram. However, several recent approaches also attempt to learn cross-lingual embeddings without pivot languages using distinct families of linguistic resources (Søgaard and Goldberg, 2016; Wu et al., 2017). Despite these efforts, we still face challenges in learning contextsensitive embeddings and incorporating cross-lingual lexical semantics. The ideal cross-lingual embedding should not only capture word meanings across languages but also be sensitive to word usage context. Words in these languages can have an infinite set of possible surface forms which complicates the availability of parallel data (Graff, 2003). Phrase-based translation methods handle this issue by tokenising the source and target languages separately (Koehn, 2009). On the other hand, well-documented solutions for morphologically rich languages include inter-layer alignment and soft word boundary handling (Galilei, 2013). Another approach is to pretrain a word-level language model (LMs) on the target language corpus.
