response: Training parallel corpora can be prohibitively expensive and time prohibitive; indeed, it can cost upwards of $1.50 per word for professional translation (Abbott, 2014). Collecting thousands of words of parallel data for a new language pair therefore requires either crowdfunding, donations, or waiting for another group to do the work. A faster alternative is to encourage translation of a new text by asking people to translate the text themselves into their native language. This makes the parallel phrase minimal, of course, as the two versions are by the same person and are likely to be duplicate even if they are not due to a translation error. This scenario, however, is closest to the situation faced by MT system combination, where the same input sentence is translated multiple times by independently running multiple translations systems. MT systems today often use neural networks trained to directly translate between two languages, and hence there is no inherent dependency relationship between the outputs of different systems. Therefore, alignment methods must be used to find a correspondence between the words or phrases from different systems. In practice, different systems sometimes produce different creative equivalent phrasings, which might be due to the different translation characteristics or even chance. The success of confusion network decoding for MT system combination (Firat et al., 2016) means that this correspondence can be represented as symbols that are shared among all translations, and hence is the expected output. The challenge of aligning these symbols while the word order can differ dramatically introduces the need for the most sophisticated hypothesis alignment methods available to the aligners. This paper is a first step towards carefully analyzing how hypothesis alignment methods impact the combination performance of multiple MT systems. We show, through empirical testing, that different alignment methods can be as good as each other under certain circumstances, but also much better or worse depending on the specific language and test set. We also propose a new method that uses a combination of forward and reverse alignments that exploit different strengths of alignment algorithms. The proposed method aligns all source sentences with all hypothesis words in the different translations. This method takes advantage of any overlap in translation that may occur, and of the fact that good alignments should be confident whenever they occur. Different alignment methods will align different things, but we can combine them all into one and then decide which items should be kept based on the strength of alignment. It uses forward and inverse word alignment between the source and target, and between the hypothesis and source. response: Training natural language parsers and semantic role labelers (SRLs) simultaneously without an inherent dependency between these two components is challenging due to two primary reasons: (i) the NLP pipeline typically features a one-way flow of information, where parsers output phrase structure (PS) representations to SRLs and do not receive feedback from the latter; and (ii) the kind of cross-modal (i.e., syntax-semantics) information required for error correction in either task is typically unavailable within pre-trained models, annotation schemes, or corpora. Here, we propose a novel set of experiments that enable the communication of cross-modal information alongside a standard NLP task. We primarily address two questions: First, can a parser learn from a full-fledged SRL, and if so, how can this be achieved? Second, can an SRL, trained to predict semantic relationships among semantic arguments (i.e., semantic roles), similarly “learn” from parsing decisions? We answer these questions through a set of experiments involving a range of models and data, including a generative parser with n-best reranking, a modularized parser that incorporates direct feedback from an SRL during parsing, and various potential versions of the SRL, including a modularized variant that receives information or even partial annotation derived from the parsing process. Throughout our experiments, we view SRL performance as a primary ground truth and hence measure the impact of each experiment specifically on SRL accuracy while also observing any secondary effects on parsing performance. Strikingly, our results show that incorporating cross-modal features derived from an integrated SRL (even through relatively simple methods such as reranking or tagging at parse time) can significantly improve SRL accuracy. Conversely, while in practice incorporating parsing constraints into the SRL leads to a degradation in its standalone performance, this degradation is minimal and can be largely mitigated by stronger models or better engineered features. These results suggest that the two models can indeed benefit from each other, and while cross-training (where both models learn together) may result in the strongest overall performance, harnessing features in a one-way dependence also yields meaningful improvements. The results are promising in that they suggest ways to leverage inter-model feedback explicitly within traditional NLP pipelines without radical changes to established approaches, and they offer technical insights into the relationship between changing the flow of dependency in existing pipelines and the outcome of these changes on core NLP tasks. A common scenario involves training a semantic role labeler (SRL) or a fine-grained parser alongside a task that acts as a “standard” or “ground truth”; for example, training the SRL on a given semantic parsing task’s outputs or predicting frame-semantic roles for entity mentions in text, while using a parser to provide syntactic analyses that the SRL might then refine. In these cases, however, the information flow is still mostly unidirectional: the parser provides structural analysis, and the SRL uses this analysis to label semantic roles. The traditional way of evaluating metrics for LG tasks relies on correlation with human judgment, but this method has several weaknesses. Human scoring is often inconsistent due to subjective judgments and lacks the necessary granularity to identify specific areas for improvement. For instance, even if a Metric A correlates better than another Metric B with human evaluations, this doesn't necessarily mean A is better in every aspect or for every possible input. Moreover, this correlation-based evaluation doesn't provide insights into why and how a metric performs better. The MUTT framework fills this gap by proposing a unit test approach for metric evaluation. It applies systematic sentence transformations (e.g., changing active to passive voice, altering tense, or modifying sentence length) as a control variable, and then measures how the evaluation metric scores change in response to these distortions. By studying the responses to these unit tests, we can gain a more nuanced understanding of each metric's strengths and weaknesses. response: Dialogue structure analysis is the study of conversational patterns or structures present in dialogue corpora. It uses these discovered structures to infer meaning from natural language communication and to improve understanding between machines and humans. It also provides a framework for building more sophisticated conversational agents. There are several methods for dialogue structure analysis proposed and used in various applications. For example, n-gram language models are widely used for statistical dialogue analysis (Ehret and Ngai, 2010;Strube and Piskorski, 2012). However, there are limitations to n-gram models for dialogue analysis. For example, they lack the ability to model higher-order latent structure (e.g., dialogue structure, long-range dependency within dialogue). Latent Markov models (LMM) and conditional random fields (CRF) are capable of modeling such latent structure (Casacuberta, 2001;Cer et al., 2008;Larsson, 2007;Strube and Piskorski, 2012) but with different limitations. One such limitation is the lack of a direct connection between different types of latent states in the hidden layer (e.g., LMM for dialogue sequential structure and CRF for global topic structure). Another is that these models are typically trained using supervised methods, which require a large amount of ground truth data for structure annotation. response: Training neural dependency parsers typically involves relying on annotated dependency structures. However, while such data is available for some languages today, nearly every major language lacks reliable and comprehensive annotations. Furthermore, supervised models may not generalize well to novel, unseen constructions. For these reasons, extensive research has been devoted to improving the performance of unsupervised dependency parsers (PDPs), which can operate without such resources. This work has often involved incorporating various types of prior knowledge about linguistic structures into the models. One particularly useful type of prior knowledge is that the parameters of grammar rules are not independent across different part-of-speech (POS) tags. Traditionally, approaches to unsupervised PDP have either used manually designed features to encode POS tag correlations or have resorted to special prior distributions, such as Dirichlet processes, which in principle can capture any correlations between structured distributions. However, among the latter approaches, there is still a dependency grammar specific to the task which constrains how well the prior can capture POS tag correlations. We propose here a novel unsupervised neural dependency parser, which instead learns such correlations implicitly via Distributed Representations (DRs). DRs are neural network outputs trained to represent POS tags. They share the common intuition that linguistic information within or across languages has implicit regularities that can be captured through common vector representations, as illustrated by work in word embeddings (Mikolov et al., 2013). Crucially, these representations are learned directly from the unlabeled corpus and so do not rely on annotations, nor on specialized prior distributions. Our approach constructs a neural network to predict the probabilities of grammar rules using as input, for each word in the sentence, the learned DR of its POS tag. The key insight is that, despite the lack of annotations, these DRs can implicitly encode POS tag correlations, since they are learned by capturing the distributional properties of POS tags across different sentences. The use of neural network models allows us to efficiently incorporate these DRs into a probabilistic framework. Specifically, our model calculates rule probabilities using a log-linear combination of the matched DRs for the words involved in the rule, weighted by learned coefficients. The outputs can be viewed as soft scores for each possible dependency and grammar rule, providing a probabilistic parse of the sentence. We compare our approach on nine languages of varying linguistic structures, using a series of experimental setups for thorough evaluation. The results indicate that our method outperforms previous unsupervised PDP methods that explicitly use POS tag correlations for information gain, as well as approaches that rely on other types of features and priors. Moreover, our approach is almost as competitive as the best supervised and semi-supervised methods in parsing accuracy when external resources, including parsers trained on other languages with different linguistic architectures, are available. response: Statistical Machine Translation (SMT) systems are known for their ability to produce translations that are fluent and have acceptable global meaning. However, these systems often fail to reproduce finer elements of language such as idiomatic expressions or less common but accepted phrases. Phrase-based SMT (PBSMT) systems are the most successful SMT systems, but they still have limitations when dealing with this kind of linguistic features (Cai and Knight, 2009). A part of the problem comes from the fact that phrase translation probabilities of PBSMT systems are computed from simple word co-occurrences. While this simplistic methodology performs surprisingly well given its simplicity, it would benefit from incorporating additional knowledge about language to better cope with more intricate linguistic features. In this article, we address the problem by introducing a novel methodology that leverages paraphrasing to improve phrase translation distributions. Our idea is simple: instead of basing the translation estimate solely on frequency co-occurrences, we propose to consider equivalent phrases that share the same meaning but are expressed differently. This approach moves us beyond the standard SMT paradigm which is primarily limited to providing translations in the rigid form of bigrams or trigrams. Our method fills this gap by proposing a sophisticated statistical framework that can identify paraphrases and intuitively utilizes them to diversify the estimated translation probabilities, making them more robust and reflecting better the different ways in which a certain meaning can be expressed in natural language. The proposed system benefits from paraphrases in two ways. First, it recognizes that semantically plausible translations can often be expressed by using different phrases or word orders, without compromising the overall meaning. This means that simply focusing on translations learned from word co-occurrences in parallel corpora can lead to missed opportunities for understanding the richer, paraphrasing complexities of language and may overlook viable translation options leading to suboptimal translations in the final output. Second, and more critically, paraphrasing helps to reduce the vocabulary sparsity issue that all SMT systems face (e.g., when translating less frequent or idiomatic phrases). By exploiting paraphrases, the system can generalize better to unseen phrases or expressions since a paraphrased form of a phrase might have enough frequency data to be more reliably estimated. response: Automatic Grammatical Error Correction (GEC) is one of the key applications of natural language processing. Given the increasing availability of data-driven approaches and computational resources, GEC has become a vibrant area of research. While the number of proposed GEC systems has grown, there is a need for a shared empirical framework to compare system performance. This paper presents the results of the first large-scale human evaluation of GEC systems. We report and analyze the results of a "gold-standard" evaluation that assembles 12 language-specific GEC systems, along with the human-annotated and unchanged input from the CoNLL-2014 shared task. We apply and extend methods used in previous human evaluation campaigns, such as those for machine translation (WMT) and verbal acceptability judgment (VAC). The produced rankings of GEC systems provide a novel dataset to measure standard metrics for semantic error correction in terms of their correlation with human judgment. The motivation for the evaluation came from the CoNLL 2014 Shared Task on Grammatical Error Correction (GEC), as well as the lack of proper evaluations in the GEC domain. While the CoNLL-2014 shared task provided an incentive for the development of GEC systems and a plethora of development data, the main evaluation metric it used was only based on automated evaluation (using BLEU as a proxy for accuracy). This approach has two main drawbacks: the use of BLEU introduces the entire uncertainty of machine translation evaluations and ignores the complex nature of grammatical error correction. Moreover, an evaluation method must consider the distinctness of linguistic rules in each target language as well as the varying complexity across different grammatical error types. response: Training natural language processing (NLP) models with annotated data is often expensive and time-consuming. To tackle these issues, various unsupervised or weakly-supervised learning techniques such as distant supervision, use of comprehensive resources like Wikipedia and Wikidata, and weak-to-strong learning have been proposed (Berant, 2011;Yıldırım et al., 2010;Huang et al., 2019). These techniques attempt to incorporate external but potentially noisy and inconsistent sources of supervision, as an alternative to or supplement to direct annotation. However, despite their potential benefits, these techniques often suffer from a number of issues due to the distant training data, including, but not limited to: (1) noisy training data, such as incorrect examples and negative examples that violate the intended semantic interpretations of relations; (2) distributions between distant labeling and semantic intended annotation tend to be imbalanced, leading to impaired generalization or partial mismatching on fine-grained aspects of the task; (3) certain information is not covered, either due to limitations of the distant data itself, or creative yet proper uses of the relation concepts are underrepresented. Temporal evidence classification, i.e., discerning whether a relational expression in text points to a specific or a generic time unit, is a key task in temporal relation extraction and is particularly problematic for distant supervision. For instance, training data for temporal evidence is difficult to collect and label, while the distributed sources such as Wikipedia or online transactional data often overrepresents general or recent events over historical events or specialized temporal units. Therefore, carefully analyzing how distinctively the distant supervision features for this task vary from the intended supervised outputs, and developing methods to address such variations, remains essential. This paper focuses on the second problem and proposes a prior-informed sampling method that can adaptively balance the distribution mismatch between distant labeling and annotated data. The intuition is the following: given different subgroups of distant labeling data that individually approximate well on certain aspects of the intended annotations but together result in an imbalanced or incomplete coverage, we can learn to weight these subgroups, effectively generating a mixed base for the learning algorithm that better approximates the true distribution of the intended outputs. The idea is inspired by techniques in transfer learning and multi-view learning but is adapted to address changing distributions across different training data sources (Mishra et al., 2017;Faruqui et al., 2014), which is a common challenge when using distant supervision. We perform extensive experiments on a temporal evidence classification dataset derived from TimeBank 3.5 (Pustejovsky et al., 2003). This dataset allows for the use of distant supervision since sufficiently large and complementary resources, including time-aligned Wikipedia and Wikidata entries, exist. We compare our method against basic distant supervision, as well as against fully supervised baselines and a temporal relation-specific reduced data set constructed from a small set of annotations. We show that our method outperforms basic distant supervision and also outperforms a purely supervised approach when evaluation metrics that are sensitive to both classification and end-to-end temporal semantic understanding are used. The contributions of this work are twofold: 1. We propose an application of prior-informed approaches to tackle the distribution mismatch issue in distantly-supervised temporal evidence classification, providing a systematic way to mix and weight different annotation sources that are supposed to capture different but partial aspects of the task. 2. response: Discourse parsing, which maps text into discourse structure, is a fundamental task in natural language processing. To date, nearly all successful systems are based on sequential dependency parsing and predict tree-like representations Moore and Carvalho (2010); van Cranenburgh et al. (2013); Amenta and Pado, 2013; questions , which are suboptimal for capturing the complex combinatorial nature of narrative discourse (Mann and Thompson, 1988; Lasnik, 1989). To better capture complex relations observed in discourse data, non-tree data structures such as Directed Acyclic Graphs (DAGs) have been proposed Mann and Thompson, 1988; Asher and Lasnik, 1993; Pustejovsky and Sanders 1995; Asher, 1999; Otter, 2002;Pitler and Niv, 2006;Welty and Strohmaier, 2008;Williams 2008, 2009, 2011; Amenta and Pado (2013, 2014), which achieve or even surpass the state-of-the-art on discourse phenomena Goldberg, 2006; Li et al., 2014; Afantenos et al., 2015; Zhou et al., 2016. However, to date, the core model for training DAG-based discourse parsers is sequential inference over dependency trees (e.g., MT (Li et al., 2014);Afantenos and Meinunger, 2016;Afantenos et al., 2015). While these methods have advanced the state-of-the-art in discourse parsing, the sequential nature of the inference models limits how much contextual information and dependencies can be modeled. Furthermore, these methods rely on approximate inference techniques (e.g. beam search or Gibbs sampling), which are often a black box, and limited to local inference. In this work, we propose to model discourse parsing as a global optimization problem, solving it using Integer Linear Programming (ILP). response: Aspect-level sentiment classification is the task of determining the sentiment expressed towards different aspects (e.g. "screen", "food", "ambiance") in a piece of text. The aspects are identified prior to sentiment analysis, and the main challenge in this task is to identify the relationships between the occurrence of the particular aspect and the sentiment expressed towards it. For questions or aspects that involve multiple context words or a larger context, most existing approaches struggle due to information loss while using coarse-grained attention mechanisms. Therefore, there is a need to utilize fractal or multi-grained attention (MGA) for better capturing of diverse context information and aspect-level interactions, which would not only enhance the accuracy but also provide a more meaningful solution to the problem. In this paper, we address the problem by introducing a Multi-grained Attention Network (MGAN), a neural network architecture derived from existing attention methods. This novel framework combines weighted aspect tokens from aspect embedding layers through multi-grained attention layers, guided by fine-grained and coarse-grained attention mechanisms. The exploration of such a multi-granularity attention mechanism allows for better control and handling of how much information from the aspect and its context is used in sentiment prediction. A key innovation of our approach is the development of an aspect-aligned loss function. This is motivated by the observation that context words for the same aspect might share similar sentimentative value. Therefore training models for each aspect separately may miss this potential aspect-level correlation. To exploit such correlation, the aspect-aligned loss encourages the model to learn consistent representations across aspects with the same context. This can lead to better generalization across distinct aspects and improve the overall performance of the model. We evaluate our proposed Multi-grained Attention Network on three different datasets: the laptop and restaurant sentiment classification tasks from the SemEval 2014 competition, and a Twitter dataset. The analysis yields consistent results across all datasets, indicating the universal applicability and effectiveness of the proposed approach. The performance improvement brought by aspect-aligned loss on all three datasets further justifies its added value in the generalizable side of aspect-level sentiment analysis. We also provide an extensive analysis of the MGAN’s decision-making process, allowing deeper insights into its inner workings and its sensitivity to different granularity levels of attention. This clarity will be beneficial to future researchers who seek to build upon or extend the framework. Furthermore, we conduct a thorough analysis of our proposed approach versus state-of-the art models, including global attention models, multi-head attention models, and aspect-specific models. This comparative analysis provides further validation of the proposed method’s superiority. In conclusion, we demonstrated the effectiveness of MGAN and its novel aspect-aligned loss function in managing and refining the aspects of attention for the task of aspect-level sentiment classification. With experimental results showing significant improvements across multiple datasets, the MGAN shows great promise as a viable new approach. This work contributes to the broader field of natural language processing for sentiment analysis, demonstrating the potential benefits of attention mechanisms that can operate over multiple granularity levels to better capture complex relationships in the text. Future research can explore various extensions of the MGAN such as using different attention mechanisms, integrating with other types of neural models, and further evaluation on more complex data sets. response: Social QA, which aims to automatically identify and extract context (the relevant discussion around an answerable question) and answer(s) of an identified query from post discussions and comments of web forums, social networks, and other large-scale social media platforms, has been gaining extensive attention in both academia and industry (Berant, 2012;Yao et al., 2013;Asri et al., 2015). The sheer scale of social media generated data makes manual moderation and annotation of content impractical and inefficient. Therefore, developing robust and flexible systems for automatic data collection and extraction is essential. While this problem is not new and similar knowledge extraction challenges were addressed in, e.g., traditional question answering (QA) or information retrieval, the unique nature of social media content - in particular, their non-standard and often informal language, as well as the dynamic nature of the content - makes this a challenging problem. Currently, many previous works in this area predominantly use traditional NLP approaches, such as various variants of logistic regression (e.g., Manning et al.,2008) or extensions of Conditional Random Fields (CRF) (e.g.,Spärck Jones and Guthrie,1995;Lafferty et al.,2001) for both context extraction and answer identification. However, such methods often fail in accurately identifying answerable questions and predicting appropriate answer while the textual structures and semantics of the online discussions are often different and varied than other more traditionally formal documents (e.g., news articles, academic papers, etc.). In this paper, we propose a novel structural Support Vector Machine (SVM) model for the task in question: i.e., to extract contexts (relevant comments, post discussions) and answers of an identified question in a large-scale online forum dataset. The essence of our approach is the redesigning the structure of input features to contextualize and semantically represent the discussion thread, allowing for more structured analysis during the decision-making or scoring process. The measured variables may include textual content, structural relations, user profile, time of posting, and other metadata whenever available. We use a Support Vector Machine (SVM) framework for our model due to its ability to perform both discriminative and generative tasks and its robustness to high-dimensional data. SVM can model complex non-linear relations using the concept of kernel functions but traditionally, in standard formulations of multi-choice and text classification, these features are normalized and combined as a large matrix, potentially losing information about the local and global structural properties of the input data. The outputs of such models can be used in a wide range of applications, from chatbots and virtual assistants to various forms of content generation, including summarization and creative writing. However, this task is particularly challenging when the input questions are drawn from a large and diverse set and the answers require a narrative structure. In this paper, we tackle the problem of generating text from structured data, using biographical text generation as a case study. The structure here refers to a fact table extracted from an external data source, such as a database or web page. Generating accurate, coherent text from such structures is a complex task for several reasons. Firstly, the relationships between individual features (or facts) in the structured source and the derived text are often complex semantic relationships. Secondly, the vocabulary needed to describe even a moderately sized domain is often extremely large, and thus it becomes challenging to train a model over such a large vocabulary. response: Word Maturity: Computational Modeling of Word Knowledge Word difficulty is a key concept in educational contexts. Words are often classified as easy or difficult, based on their frequency of use or the ease with which they can be understood. While current corpus-based measures of word difficulty offer a starting point for this classification, they fall short in several key areas. Firstly, current metrics are scalar, providing only a single difficulty score for each word, and fail to capture the complexity of word understanding, which varies greatly across different aspects of language learning. Second, they are divorced from theoretical understandings of how learners acquire language. Therefore, they fail to account for the changes in word understanding that occur as knowledge develops over time. At any stage of language acquisition, there is a range of words for which the learner may possess some level of understanding - perhaps recognizing its form, having a nascent sense of its meaning, or being able to use it in a limited way. However, the precise state of each word's knowledge in a learner's internal lexicon is complex and nuanced, and its difficulty arises from a variety of factors including its form, how it relates to the learner's existing knowledge, and how it is used in language. As such, it is reasonable to consider not just the difficulty or ease of words but also the progressive stages of this acquisition, what we term 'word maturity'. A conceptually mature word might be understood with multiple layers of nuance and assumed in the context of other words. In contrast, a less mature word may be only partially recognized or understood in a limited context. To address these limitations, we introduce the concept of word maturity, a computational model that aims to track the degree of knowledge of each word at different stages in language learning, from early vocabulary development to advanced understanding of the words and their contexts. Our model, Word Maturity, is based on a theoretical understanding that language acquisition is a gradual and iterative process that builds on existing knowledge. It is informed by psycho- and cognitive linguistics, specifically by Saussure's notion of sign (signifier, signified) and a later extension by Halliday to account for the role of context in word meaning ( Halliday & Hasan, 1990). A central hypothesis of our approach is that each word's readiness for use varies across different learning contexts and stage of language acquisition. This readiness is not only a function of frequency or accessibility but also of depth of meaningful experience. For example, a learner might learn a word through direct instruction, through use in context, or through deduction from related words. Each of these acquisition types may lead to a distinct level of maturity. The Word Maturity model predicts the degree to which a word can be effectively used in communication. A highly mature word can be used with a substantial degree of nuance and predictability in a wide range of contexts. In contrast, a less mature word may be used without full understanding or precision, or only in very specific contexts. LSA, a widely used method for analyzing large corpora, maps words, text, and parameters of meaning onto a common space. response: Social media platforms have become the default mode of communication in modern society. Not only do people's online interactions increase our understanding of their social networks, beliefs, and values but such information can also be leveraged to study broader social phenomena and psychological phenomena that occur within individuals. One such social–psychological phenomenon that may be observed in online interactions is dogmatism—a rigid conviction in one's beliefs and an unwillingness to consider opposing perspectives. Empirical research (e.g., Altemeyer, 2006; Kuran and Sunstein, 1999; Rosenblum et al., 1980) has identified key characteristics of dogmatic individuals. For example, dogmatic individuals often display a lack of critical thinking, intolerance to differing viewpoints, overconfidence, and a tendency to engage in extreme beliefs that have been empirically derived to affect behavior. Uncovering dogmatism in social media data could contribute to the understanding of the spread of misinformation and the polarizing effects of online interactions. As such, the project's aim is to identify linguistic and behavioral signals of dogmatism in online discourse through statistical modeling. To build models that predict dogmatism in user comments, we will leverage crowdsourced annotations and leverage existing theories from psychology. Our work utilizes a corpus of annotated Reddit posts and examines dogmatic behavior across a diverse set of conversational topics. We use a cognitive linguistic approach to identify verbal expressions indicative of dogmatic attitudes. Specifically, we look for overt signals of confidence, intolerance to debate or disagreement, and absolute language used by individuals (e.g., overuses of "always", "never", qualifying statements such as "clearly", "obviously", and in-group/out-group labels). Additionally, we consider the discourse dynamics and the contexts in which these expressions occur, aiming to model the intricacies of real-world language use where signals of dogmatism are often embedded in nuanced and context-dependent textual cues. Our predictive models will combine these linguistic features with behavioral signals of dogmatism, such as the tendency to post content that refrains from questioning one's own beliefs or the propensity to regularly interact with posts advocating extreme or unyielding viewpoints. A key innovation in our approach involves explicitly operationalizing some core features of dogmatism (as described in psychological theory) into measurable features. response: Social media platforms, online forums, and various other electronic communication services present a fertile ground for simultaneous online conversations. Many today's social media platforms enable people to engage in multiple conversation threads at once, and use of these services gives rise to a various forms of interleaved conversations. As voice-user interfaces are on the rise, the number of applications that enable simultaneous conversations is expected to increase further. In conversations involving multiple participants and where statements are interwoven, messages may "jump" between different threads. Such conversations often interleave threads, where each participant may pick up and respond to older messages while also pursing new ones. When processing this type of interlinear text, knowledge of the conversation structure, and more importantly the nesting of responses – the hierarchical structure of the verbal exchange – can greatly aid in understanding individual messages in context. This knowledge is also valuable to applications like digital personal assistants that aim to engage in coherent discussions with human users by keeping track of multiple conversational threads. Disentanglement of interleaved threaded conversations is thus a problem known to date mainly from user interface studies and computational linguistics. In user interface research, ensembling over multiple threads can lead to various applications such as thread ranking, summarization or simply sequential thread representation, which presumably orients the user intuitively For instance, a ranked list of message threads view might help a user focus on their salient issues first. Conversational message disentanglement is still largely an unsolved problem. Traditional text processing techniques such as dependency parsing can help to some extent, but are hindered by variables such as an inability to distinguish message boundaries or to infer conversation nesting. The most common previous approaches to disentangling conversation structure include : 1. Lexical similarity: Maps each message to another based on the words and their contexts they share . 2. Structural similarity: Analyses the dependencies between words in each message . 3. Temporal analysis: Uses the time or sequence of messages to infer thread boundaries . The principle shortcomings of these approaches appear to hinge around their limitations to analyze context together with structure. Specifically, the meaning of a message often cannot be fully understood without considering both the words used and the explicitly stated or implied context governing those words. We address this limitation by proposing an approach that leverages changing contextual properties to expand the meaning representation of messages. Our approach uses a probabilistic message expansion that considers both explicit and hidden context features. Our hypothesis for success hinges on the fact that when messages are intertwined so as to make them difficult to separate, the explicit and hidden contextual information i.e., surrounding words, previous messages, the speaker ID, and the topic of the conversation, may provide clues towards de-interlacing the conversation . Common examples of hidden context include whether a word or phrase is typical for a given participant, or if particular terms are strongly associated with certain conversation topics. Explicit context might be information often disclosed or inferred in the conversation such as prior topics or any mention of a named reference entity like the user, participant, or a subject of the conversation . Our specific solution, dubbed message expansion for disentanglement (MED), extends a message across its context to better capture its meaning and conversational parameters which can then help group messages into separate conversations. The key innovation is successful integration of context-based probabilistic inference into each expanded message which would enables better differentiation among messages and therefore better thread separation. Traditional topic models such as Latent Dirichlet Allocation (LDA) work at a coarse granularity level, capturing word co-occurrence at the document or sentence level and can thus only identify general topics relevant to the corpus. In contrast, word embedding methods such as Word2Vec and Glove model word co-occurrence within small sliding windows, resulting in embeddings that capture fine-grained semantic relationships between words. The proposed Latent Topic Embedding (LTE) model keeps the advantages of topic modeling and word embedding while allowing for knowledge integration across various word co-occurrence levels. LTE achieves this by learning latent topics at different granularity levels and simultaneously generating word embeddings from these topics. This allows for a richer representation of both topic diversity and the intricacies of word semantics. LTE is grounded on the observation that each word tends to appear in different contexts (space and time) which indicates different aspects of its meaning. By factorizing the topics and word embeddings simultaneously, LTE can learn latent topics that are more nuanced and coherent while still retaining spatial and temporal constraints on word co-occurrences. This approach enriches the topic model by incorporating word embeddings, which can capture both syntactic and semantic relationships. Our model includes three main components: the topic model, the embedding model, and the inference algorithm. The topic model learns topics in a way that incorporates the embedding information to increase model coherence and relevance. This results in more interpretable topics, as the model captures semantic relationships naturally present in the data. While tree-adjoining grammar models can model certain kinds of syntactic and semantic dependencies, they are typically not designed to handle the diverse and varied contexts in which words occur. The embedding model leverages the latent topics learned from the first part to generate distributional word embeddings that reflect different aspects of a word's meaning, depending on the context in which it is used. This embedding step refines and extends the information captured by traditional word embedding algorithms by relating words not just to local contexts, but to broader latent topics. By integrating these two processes within a unified framework, LTE aims to create a more comprehensive representation of semantic knowledge than either traditional word embedding or topic modeling techniques alone. The results show that LTE outperforms state-of-the-art models in tasks such as document classification, text similarity, and word semantic relatedness. It deals with dividing a Chinese text into individual words or morphemes based on language rules and context. As Chinese questions are not separated by spaces, this process is vital for further NLP tasks such as machine translation, named entity recognition, sentiment analysis, and question answering, among others. Most state-of-the-art word segmentation methods for Chinese are based on supervised learning, which keeps improving as more annotated corpora become available (Song et al., 2013). However, acquiring annotated corpora is a costly and time-consuming process, and often, domain-specific corpora may not be easily available or cannot be derived directly from available annotated general-purpose corpora. As a result, these supervised methods can fail when we need to segment new texts from different domains or even texts with out-of-vocabulary (OOV) words where annotated corpus data is not available. Currently, several methods have been proposed to tackle these issues. One common approach is to leverage general-domain annotated corpora for achieving domain-adaptation, which often relies on domain-specific feature engineering or re-training with domain-specific data (He et al., 2016; Li et al., 2016). However, the performance of such adaptations can still be limited by the availability and quality of domain-specific examples, not to mention the specialized expertise required for feature engineering or careful selection of appropriate out-of-domain features for re-training. Another promising direction, especially for word segmentation, is to expand available annotated corpora for more general cross-domain adaptation by adding data from a different but related domain and fine-tuning a model using the combined dataset (Hill et al., 2016; Walther et al., 2017). However, expanding corpora in this way can only be effective if such related data is truly available and relevant, which may not always be the case, particularly for highly specialized or domain-specific word usage. Therefore, we propose a novel corpus expansion method for Chinese word segmentation that confronts these challenges by exploiting the vast, diverse, and changing online content. response: Training natural language processing (NLP) models on large-scale datasets is inherently challenging due to the cost of processing time. Chinese word segmentation is one such task that requires handling a large vocabulary of characters and their corresponding segmentation information. Moreover, when training for new word detection, we have to handle new words or out-of-vocabulary (OOV) words which are not present in the training data. This further increases the complexity and size of the dataset. Training a model with a large number of parameters and features, therefore, can become very computationally expensive and time-consuming, especially when combined with new word detection. Therefore, there is a need for a fast and efficient training method. In this paper, we present an online training method for Chinese word segmentation and new word detection that is based on adapting the learning rate of features based on their frequency of occurrence in the training dataset. The method we propose is based on the idea of faster convergence in frequency regions where the training data is well represented. As a result, it allows the model to quickly converge on the known word boundaries and reduce the number of iterations required to reach a suitable accuracy. As a general purpose optimization method, our approach can be useful in a wide range of NLP tasks that involve large scale data or high dimensional features. By reducing the time required to train a model, it can potentially increase the productivity of researchers and developers working in the field. Our contribution is threefold: 1. **Joint Modeling for Chinese Word Segmentation and New Word Detection**: We present a model that incorporates both the standard word segmentation features and additional features for new word detection, effectively making it possible to learn from the same set of training data for both tasks simultaneously in an elegant way. 2. **Adaptive Online Gradient Descent with Frequency-aware Learning Rates**: To tackle the issue of slow training due to large scale and high dimensional features, we redesign the training algorithm to adaptively change the learning rates based on the frequency of features in the training data. This potentially makes such Chinese NLP models more accessible and useful for practical applications. Secondly, by demonstrating the performance of our fast training method on the combined task of word segmentation and new word detection, we reveal its potential for a broader range of NLP architectures and tasks. We will then describe the experimental setup and the results, including the comparison with state-of-the-art methods. Finally, we will discuss the limitations of our method, avenues for future work, and the broader implications across NLP research and applications. We note that the method described is not specific to Chinese word segmentation or new word detection but can be applied to any NLP model training where frequency information could be useful, such as in other segmentation tasks (e.g., tokenization in English) or NLP models involving high-dimensional feature vectors. However, while such data's cost and availability scale with the number of supported languages, language-specific parsers' inference complexity scales with deep features of language structure. This unrealistic alignment motivates universal parsing, where a single parser can handle all languages and, through this, utilize a larger size of corpora. A universal parser is trained on multilingual data where each sentence's language is known, offering a generalization to new languages. The inference cost, however, suffers the same fractal complexity properties of language observed in monolingual parser. Therefore, a more scalable alternative can be a language-agnostic parser, knowledgeably ignorant to word order, but still powerful enough to leverage the universality of human language structure, such as argument structure or functional compositionality. Sentence meaning must, nonetheless, be shaped to specific semantic roles via question-answering sample pairs following a particular schema - "who", "what", "when", etc., which amounts to a form of controlled semantic space known to natural language processing (NLP) as a "slot". While such a system would require little modification for similar sentences in various languages, it cannot discern possible answers without schemas typed in English - relying on both the slot mapping and the word-form mapping between English and the target language. Our work proposes an approach towards universal slot-based question answering (UB-Question), specifically designed for multilingual interfaces of knowledge-graph-based systems. In this work, we interpret the "universal" not as the training data's universality (multilingual corpora without syntactic annotations), but as the universal grammar (Hualde, 2014) and shared ontological principles of human concepts across languages (Fellbaum, 1998). To that end, we harness the vast availability of schema-grounded question-and-answer (QA) pairs, which we call 'complex questions', to build understanding on all languages based on structured arguments (e.g., events or roles) of measured variables - together called 'attributes'. However, traditional NLP tools, including indispensable tagging systems like part-of-speech (POS) and named entity taggers (NER), struggle to generalize well to contemporary texts due to various factors such as the informal nature of social media, short sentences and text fragments, and language of various quality levels. response: Grammatical error detection (GED) is a fundamental task in natural language processing (NLP) that has been proven useful in various settings, such as second language instruction, language learning, and machine translation (Krishnan and van Veen, 2016). In educational contexts, it is used to provide feedback to language learners, suggesting corrections and promoting learning (Biber and Conrad, 2009). Similarly, in machine translation, GED can improve generated translations by preemptively correcting likely errors, enhancing the overall quality of the service (Koehn and Monz, 2006). As with many NLP tasks, the accuracy and applicability of a GED system are best evaluated through systematic comparison with a reliable baseline or with other GED systems, ideally using a shared benchmark. This necessitates consistent and reliable ways to evaluate GED systems. The task of GED, however, presents several challenges making the process of evaluation more complex compared to other NLP tasks. On one hand, the nature of grammatical errors—various in type and often creative—makes it difficult to rigidly define and accurately detect them. Offense and defense in error detection also complicates the task. For example, a sentence might contain multiple grammatical errors, and this is common. The number and type of errors can vary greatly even between sentences in the same corpus. A system may correctly identify one error but miss another. Moreover, the written language itself is often flexible and nuances within it allow sentences deemed "grammatically incorrect" by one standard or person to be acceptable (and perhaps preferred) under another (Biber and Conrad, 2009; Biber, 2010). An evaluator, therefore, must carefully consider contexts and standards when assessing "errors." These factors make the task inherently problematic for evaluation. 1. True Positives, False Negatives, False Positives and True Negatives: The most straightforward yet fundamental aspects of the problem relate to basic metrics of measured evaluation: true positives (correctly identified errors), false positives (incorrectly identified non-errors as errors), true negatives (correctly identified non-errors as non-errors), and false negatives (missed errors). Because a language changing according to context and function calls for a nuanced view of errors, these raw measurements allow evaluation on a case-by-case basis. A standard for what constitutes an "error" needs to be defined clearly and consistently, such as using widely accepted language standards or predefined error types in a corpus. However, this still does not fully address the complexities of language flexibility and context dependency. Many systems overuse the use of F1 scores or accuracy as sole measures, which can inherently be misleading. For instance, a system that does not detect any errors (producing many false negatives) but also does not produce any false positives could receive a high F1 score, which while mathematically valid, is practically misleading. Therefore, reporting raw data is encouraged to give a clearer picture of a system's performance, alongside traditional measures if using them. 2. response: Training Hybrid Models with Pragmatically Enriched Word and Subword Representations for Dialog System Performance We present a novel approach for training pragmatic word and subword representations for use in spoken language understanding (SLU) systems. Subword units are well-suited for open vocabulary recognition (Vinyals et al., 2015, Chorowski et al., 2014), and have been incorporated into deep learning-based dialog and speech recognition systems (He et al., 2016, Chorowski and Glembek, 2016, Baevski and Auli, 2018). These subwords are often generated using routine subword splitting techniques, such as those used to create wordpieces (Vinyals et al., 2015) or Byte Pair Encoding (BPE) (Sennrich et al., 2016). These subwords are typically built over large pre-existing corpora, such as Wikipedia. PragmaticallyAnnotated SLU datasets (e.g., Switchboard, CALLHOME) are vital for dialog and spoken language understanding research, providing hundreds of thousands of training examples and enabling models to learn various pragmatic and conversational behaviors. However, previous work has ignored their use in creating or training subword unit lexicons, so that this contextually rich and specific information provided by these datasets is not fully leveraged in the subword structures. In this paper, we propose the use of pragmatic information from pragmaticallyannotated datasets at the time of subword model building (Figure 1). We show that incorporating pragmatically-annotated data during subword model creation can lead to better SLU performance, especially for retrieval-based dialog system tasks in which the nuanced contexts inferred through pragmatic annotation are essential. 1 We focus on spoken language and face-to-face dialog contexts, leading to subword units that are candidates for the representation of user desires in conversational dialog systems. 2 We use subword units that are pragmaticallyannotated in training corpora, creating rich subword contexts measured by features such as discourse functions and salience. We first outline the fundamentals of subword modeling and SLU, highlighting the value of contextualization in dialog performance. We then present our framework and describe the technical details of extracting pragmatic word and subword features from annotated corpora and incorporate these into pre-training of hybrid models combining word and subword embeddings. We show that our pragmatically-annotated subword units outperform baseline models (blindly trained on large zero-context data) on several SLU benchmarks designed to gauge understanding under various pragmatic considerations. The insights and empirical results of this work could have implications for real-world platforms where conversational understanding and freedom from closed-vocabulary constraints are of the essence. ### 2. Core Concepts and Contributions The core of our contribution lies in the way we treat subwords as enriched symbolic units carrying pragmatic properties derived directly from pragmatically-annotated corpora. We first clarify why this approach is necessary and beneficial for spoken dialog SLU systems: - *Performance Gap*: By leveraging pragmatically enriched subwords, our model can better understand nuanced context that, otherwise, might be difficult to infer from word-token-level meaning. - *Open Vocabulary*: Subwords naturally extend the vocabulary size without the need for manual expansion or exceptions, crucial for tasks involving fast-paced, real-world dialog, where new words or word usages can rapidly emerge. - *Efficient Semantic Representation*: Pragmatically annotated subwords can capture meaningful relationships and contexts at various lingual scales between word, phrase, clause, and even utterance levels

response: Training bilingual sentiment word embeddings (BSWE) that capture both semantic meaning and sentiment information is crucial for efficient cross-language sentiment classification (CLSC). In this paper, we present an approach to learn BSWE for English-Chinese CLSC. Unlike previous work that exploits large-scale parallel corpora, our proposed framework can be trained even when a small size of monolingual labeled corpora and their translations are available. Through systematically empirical and theoretical investigation, we demonstrate that incorporating sentiment information into bilingual embeddings leads to improved CLSC performance, as our proposed B-SWE can better leverage and map semantically similar words even if they are not exactly equivalent in meaning across languages due to distinct linguistic structures and cultural influences, and more importantly capture sentiment nuances in a more effective way. These BSWE can also benefit a variety of downstream NLP tasks that involve both source and target language inputs, including among others, machine translation, question answering, and dialogue systems. The remainder of the paper is organized as follows. Section 2 presents relevant background on CLSC, sentiment word embeddings and bilingual sentiment analysis. Section 3 describes the proposed B-SWE framework, including the sentiment-inclusive training objective and potential model architectures. Section 4 details the experimental setup, including data preparation and experimental protocol. Finally, Section 5 presents the experimental results on NLP&CC 2013 CLSC dataset, along with analysis of the proposed approach and comparison with the state of the art. Conclusions are in Section 6. 2 Background Sentiment classification aims at classifying the polarity of a given text (e.g., positive, negative or neutral) (Pang & Lee, 2004). The performance in this task largely depends on sentiment resources, which are typically labeled datasets and lexical resources. However, these resources are imbalanced across different languages: English and Chinese are well-resourced with sentiment analysis datasets, but many other languages are not. Therefore, to build high-quality sentiment classifiers for resource-scarce languages, one possible solution is to transfer knowledge from English or Chinese, a task referred to as cross-language sentiment classification (CLSC). For example, if we want to build a sentiment classifier for Japanese but only have a small labeled dataset in Japanese, we could leverage English-Japanese parallel corpora and English labeled datasets to build a model that can classify Japanese sentiment effectively (Nie & Chen, 2014; Wu et al., 2018). Bilingual word embeddings (BWE) (Artetxe et al., 2016; Johnson et al., 2017; Yasunaga et al., 2018) are widely used in CLSC and other NLP tasks involving languages other than English (e.g., cross-lingual information retrieval (XIR) (Smith & Lin, 2017), cross-lingual dependency parsing (Yin & He, 2018)). These embeddings are generated based purely on parallel corpora, with the goal of placing semantically similar words closer in the vector space, regardless of their languages. They are especially useful for low-resource languages where large monolingual corpora may not be available. However, word embeddings trained only on text data might not capture successful sentiment information. Thus, previous work has incorporated sentiment information into embeddings (3, 4, 5). While these works demonstrate the capability of embedding vectors to capture both semantic meaning and sentiment, they do not address the CLSC scenario where sentiment corpora are also language-specific and often of limited size. 3 Bilingual Sentiment Word Embeddings Framework

Some of the most notable examples of such setups include the work of Lazaridou et al. (2017), who proposed an "Emergent Communication via Multi-Agent Interaction". In this study, the authors demonstrated that agents could indeed develop a grounded communication protocol purely through multi-agent interaction, without any human intervention, by exploring object configurations within a visual scene and seeking to communicate about them. However, the focus of these and similar works has been primarily on the language itself - the symbols, or "utterances," that agents use or learn to use. Less attention has been given to the question of what these symbols denote, or how these agents "see" the world visually, which is a fundamental requirement if we are to understand the true capacities and limitations of emergent communication systems. Furthermore, understanding the visual representations used by agents in such emergent language games has implications far beyond language itself. It points to the fundamental question of how AI systems might generalize learned knowledge across different tasks or representations in visual or other sensory contexts. If agents develop strong generalizations in terms of language, but these generalizations are not reflected in their understanding of the visual world, it could suggest that the agents' learning mechanisms are focusing more on the linguistic aspects of the game rather than on the conceptual understanding or visual semantics of the world around them. Traditional Arabic language processing systems, including those for morphological analysis and disambiguation, are often trained on standard or literary Arabic and may fail to perform adequately on dialectal texts due to this noise and structural divergence. response: Training neural machine translation (NMT) models at a prohibitive cost in terms of time and computational resources remains one of the major obstacles in applying NMT to practical tasks. State-of-the-art deep NMT models, particularly Sequence-to-Sequence (Seq2Seq) models with attention (Bahdanau et al., 2014; Luong et al., 2015), are known to require hundreds of thousands of sentences for training and may need several days to a week even on modern GPU-equipped machines. Such models are out of reach for many applications and setups, especially when real-time latency is required. To address this problem, various approaches have been proposed to make NMT models smaller. Knowledge distillation (KD) is one such technique that had been successfully applied to reduce the size of neural networks in image classification (Hinton et al., 2015; Romero et al., 2014). KD works by using the parameters and predictions of a large teacher model as a form of supervised data to train a smaller student model with fewer parameters. However, most existing knowledge distillation work in the NMT domain focus on similar word-level prediction as the teacher model. This paper proposes to extend the knowledge distillation idea to both the word-level and the sequence-level predictions of a teacher NMT model and examines their effectiveness for both size reduction and performance preservation. We introduce two novel sequence-level knowledge distillation (seq2seq KD) methods. The first introduces the entire teacher’s output distribution as a prior for the probabilities over the student model’s outputs, and the second carefully estimates how similar (in a specific statistical way) the student model's distribution should be to the teacher model’s. Attention mechanisms inherently assume knowledge about what to attend, limiting generalization to unseen relationships. They can also become computationally expensive for large inputs, and their capacity for capturing complex interactions may be limited. Furthermore, their learned weights often reveal relationships among semantic features beyond simple attention weighted sums but do not provide a principled way to model how these features interact. Hence, while attention models achieve strong results, they often do not provide clear interpretability regarding the interactions and paths through which they evaluate entailment. Recent advances have introduced the use of convolution neural networks (CNNs) to predict entailment between sentences (Williams et al., 2018). CNNs provide a means to universally apply filters and view symbols within a sentence through these filters simultaneously, hence capturing the local and compositional structure of sentences. However, the mainstream application of CNNs to NLI has been as a two-layer model (with the sentence features followed by an attention layer). Twitter’s facility for open and real-time discourse provides a unique forum for citizens to express their opinions about other nations and international affairs. response: Social media platforms have become the preferred mode of communication for people worldwide. Each demographic, from teenagers to grandparents, uses social media; these platforms have become an integral part of everyday life. Hence, social media data provides a rich source for understanding various sociographical aspects of language use, including expressions of sentiment. However, the language variations among different demographics in social media are not yet fully explored. This is a vital gap in improving multilingual sentiment analysis (MSA) models. While the field of MSA has seen considerable advancements, most research focuses on generic (and often American-centric) data extracted from online sources that can be less representative of global societal nuances, particularly those dependent on demographic factors, such as gender and age. The vocabulary, linguistic structure, emoticons, and even the use of hashtags can differ significantly between demographics, even within the same language. For instance, younger speakers may use slang or more acronyms, while older generations might be more formal or use less common expressions of sentiment such as the greater use of positive words with negative sentiment. Gender also plays a role in language use, with studies showing significant differences in the frequency of certain emotive or sensational terms between male and female English speakers (Pennebaker, 2011). We hypothesize that there are similar gender-based language variations across languages, such as different emoticon preferences or use of positive/negative polarizing words. The exploration of such demographic language variations in social media data can significantly enrich and improve sentiment analysis models across languages. This paper focuses on exploiting gender differences in sentiment language for three languages: English, Spanish, and Russian. Additionally, we explore cross-cultural differences in emoticon and hashtag use as these elements are often underutilized by existing MSA models. We extract large-scale Twitter datasets in these languages and apply unsupervised techniques to identify gender-specific language patterns. We then train models to leverage these differences for polarity and subjectivity classification. Our hypothesis is that by incorporating these demographic nuances, MSA models can better capture sentiments, particularly in previously understudied languages, cultures, or subgroups within a language. Our experiments show statistically significant relative F-measure improvements for both polarity and subjectivity classification by considering gender in MSA. For example, English sees a 2.5% and 5% relative improvement for polarity and subjectivity respectively, while Russian improves by 1.5% and 1% for polarity and subjectivity, and Spanish improves by 2% and 0.5% for the same tasks. Furthermore, we investigate the use of emoticons and hashtags across gender. These elements are almost universally used in expressing sentiment in social media, yet they are often neglected in MSA models, particularly for languages other than English (Pang et al., 2002). Our results show that the prevalence and types of emoticon use differ between genders, with females using more emotive and positive-emotional emoticons while males use more sarcastic ones. Similarly, preferences for certain hashtags (e.g., those related to fashion vs. sports) tend to differ by gender. These findings present a new direction in MSA research that can potentially improve sentiment analysis across languages and cultures. To encourage future research, we release our annotated datasets and models, which can be used to extend these gender-based models to other languages or to explore other demographic variations. In particular, rating scores have become a focal point for analyzing and understanding the sentiment of user-generated content. While user ratings have been well studied for their individual value, their role in machine learning tasks is relatively under-examined, particularly with regard to sentiment analysis questions. This paper investigates the reproducibility of sentiment ratings from text. A central question we examine is whether humans can accurately infer the sentiment rating (e.g., 1-5 stars) of text (e.g., movie reviews) when provided with an empty rating field alongside the text content. This scenario mimics common training data scenarios in sentiment analysis, where texts are accompanied by human-derived ratings. If humans can reliably reconstruct a rating based on the text alone, then the text contains valuable information about the rating, which could be used to train classification models for sentiment or rating prediction. If we can also compare human accuracy to machine performance, it could serve as a baseline for understanding the predictability of text content with respect to sentiment and rating. Furthermore, if human and machine performance are comparable, we could suggest approaches for extracting potential useful features from text for scoring or rating systems. We also investigate a less-explored question: whether the source of a rating (whether from the original author or from an independent annotator) significantly impacts machine learning models' performance when assumed to represent the 'true' sentiment label. This question arises from a substantial body of literature that has documented variability in human annotations and ratings across different tasks (e.g., sentiment, topic labeling, or tagging (Etzioni et al., 2011;Goldberg, 2017)). If differences exist, we should also consider the implications for training machine learning models that might need to generalize across different sources of sentiment labeling. To answer these questions, we conducted an analysis using a publicly available dataset of IMDb movie reviews, supplemented with crowd-sourced annotations. Each review in our dataset includes original author-provided ratings as well as independently re-labeled crowd-sourced ratings. Resolution modes capture semantic relationships between mentions such as equality (John met with Ron, where Ron and John refer to the same person), modification (the city in the US, where "the city" and "the US refer to the same location or entity), and contiguity (Tom met with Harry, on the day he visited New York, where "the day" is the time when "Tom" visited "New York"). These platforms can reveal consumer sentiment, market trends, and potential business opportunities. With millions of users posting about a wide range of topics daily, microblogs can serve as a powerful voice of the consumer. In particular, identifying potential trend related products before they surge in popularity could be a powerful way for businesses to gain a competitive edge. A trend can be any phenomenon that gains widespread popularity among the public, often accompanied by increased consumer demand. Examples of such trends include popular movies and TV shows, viral social movements, celebrity endorsements, and changes in societal beliefs or behaviors (e.g., the increased demand for vegetarian products due to animal rights awareness). For e-commerce businesses, recognizing these trends early and acting upon them can lead to significant gains, as companies can adjust their product offerings, marketing strategies, and possibly even supply chains in anticipation of the trend. Identifying trend-related products requires a multifaceted approach that considers both the temporal nature of trends and the complex semantics involved in microblog content. However, mining microblog data for commercial intents and associated trends is challenging. Microblog posts are typically short and noisy, with their content often filled with abbreviations, slang, sarcasm, and context-specific references. Despite this noise, microblog posts contain valuable information about consumer preferences, criticisms, and other form of user feedback. Our algorithm aims to capture the commercial intents hidden in microblog posts using graph-based methods while leveraging the temporal nature of trends. We show how our approach can model not only the relevance of a product to a trend but also the associativity of that product with contexts related to the trend. response: Training natural language understanding (NLU) models with vision or any other grounded information requires an inherent cost. Grace (2017) identified three core challenges for grounded NLU: data insufficiency, use of weak supervision, and unrealistic training objectives. While weak supervision (e.g., crowdsourcing or other forms of indirect feedback, as opposed to gold-standard supervision) can alleviate the data insufficiency issue (Asri et al., 2017; Blukis et al., 2018; Xiong et al., 2016), it still poses significant challenges for model training and evaluation. When training with weak supervision, model evaluation becomes particularly error-prone, as any discrepancy between the gold-standard (but unavailable) output and the model's output cannot be used for training. A common approach to address this issue is to rerank model outputs among semanticly comparable alternatives, weighted by a generator (such as a language model) to mimic the feedback from a human evaluator (Bansal et al., 2008; Xiong et al., 2020). However, the reranker often struggles to learn good ranking weights from weak feedback. In this paper, we propose adapting discriminative or output-based reranking techniques For grounded language learning problems. In such tasks, symbols provided by weak supervision (e.g., a "reward" signal indicating task success), though binary or limited in scope, can guide the reranking process. We argue that even within the limitations of weak feedback, training discriminative reranking models can improve model performance by (i) prioritizing higher-likelihood answers that are semantically more plausible given the context or previous model predictions, and (ii) maintaining discriminative scores across different training objectives (e.g., task completion vs. reference tree similarity) leading to stronger generalization. We present an approach that adapts discriminative reranking to utilize weak supervision signals and provide an experimental evaluation on a grounded instruction following task. The primary contribution of this work is demonstrating that the discriminative reranking approach can effectively improve the performance of grounded NLU models, even in the presence of weak supervision. response: Training natural language understanding (NLU) models that can understand unstructured instructions and produce an executable plan remains a significant challenge. The majority of existing NLU systems are designed for well-defined tasks with deeply studied structure (e.g., down-selected actions, limited vocabulary, fixed relationships between entities). For navigation tasks though, the system’s response is not entirely determined by questions or commands asked by the user (e.g., "go straight and turn left at the corner "), but also depends on the current state and the environment of the robot as well as past interactions with the user (e.g., "how do I get to the right"). This complexity is compounded in public space settings where users may provide instructions with varying levels of detail, clarity, and specificity. For example, if I ask: "Can you take me to McDonald’s?" the system is expected to know not only the current location of the robot, but also the locations of "me", the starting and ending points of the tour (space and time), and preferences/constraints (e.g., user preference for walking paths or shortest path conditions). If the system already has information about "McDonald’s", it can reply "Sure, it's 300 meters away at your 6 o'clock. Now turn left and head this way." Whereas, if it encounters a new entity, "McDonald’s" for the first time during this conversation, it would typically fail to give an actionable response. In this paper, we propose a model that translates free-form natural language instructions by the user into a high-level navigation plan for a robot in a multi-floor building space. Our approach is summarised in Figure 1 in Section 3. We assume that user instructions are provided through natural language (e.g., "Turn right and go to the right door"). Our model converts this input into a sequence of high-level navigation directions that can be executed by a robot controller (e.g., "go to (x, y)"). The problem we solve is to map natural language utterances to this sequence of high-level actions. Our model leverages a topological representation of the environment to bridge the gap between natural language instructions and low-level navigation commands. We also argue that a systematic understanding of concepts in natural language instructions is critical in bridging this gap. For instance, prepositions like "to", "at", "near", and "along" can have drastic implications on navigation directions in different contexts. A high-level navigation plan must accurately account for such distinctions if it is to be informative and useful for the robot. Our method incorporates attention mechanisms to emphasize relationships between navigation directions and topological features of the environment in the form of a map. As such, we evaluate our model on a new dataset that contains example natural language utterances paired with corresponding navigation plans. We provide a compositional parser that maps each continuous text to a series of high-level navigation actions, while also presenting a novel evaluation metric for natural language-based navigation planning. We conclude that the proposed model, which incorporates a topological representation of the environment, outperforms baseline approaches and establishes a new SOTA for the navigation planning task. Our conclusion builds confidence in the feasibility of training systems that can effectively translate human instructions into actionable navigation plans, opening up research avenues for further functional successful integration with real-world robots. Overall, this study contributes to the objective of enabling natural language interaction with robots in real-world settings, a prerequisite for future systems to effectively assist humans with task execution in diverse environments. This is a work in progress. Further analysis on handling ambiguity, user errors, and more complex, dynamic environments would be presented in upcoming sections
